meta.name: After Effects 25.6 — Windows Complete Learning Manual
meta.provenance: Adobe release history, 25.x system requirements, Adobe documentation and user-supplied 26.5 topic inventory curated to 25.6

stagePlan.name: Orientation
stagePlan.objective: Build and navigate a correctly saved composition, understand sources and place layers precisely.
stagePlan.gate: From a blank project, recreate a 4-second two-card edit, relink a source and identify Position versus Anchor Point.
stagePlan.practice: Create a small working scene from solids, text and one imported source.

stagePlan.name: Animation and compositing basics
stagePlan.objective: Animate deliberately and understand how paths, mattes, text, precomps and effects change the image.
stagePlan.gate: Build a 4-second title reveal with at least two eased properties, a track matte, a named precomp, and a deliberate effect order.
stagePlan.practice: Try the loading-ring, text-window and logo-reveal recipes.

stagePlan.name: Real footage and production craft
stagePlan.objective: Work with sound, keying, tracking, 3D space, color and basic controller expressions.
stagePlan.gate: Complete a short moving-footage composite, inspect every frame for track drift or alpha errors, and link a visible property to a controller.
stagePlan.practice: Try a Keylight, a point track, and an audio-reactive exercise.

stagePlan.name: Reusable and complex systems
stagePlan.objective: Make data-driven templates, control 3D/model interactions, use Puppet and native particle tools, and automate repetitive edits safely.
stagePlan.gate: Create one editable template with independent instances plus a separate reproducible procedural/3D or scripted experiment.
stagePlan.practice: Try the reusable lower third, JSON scoreboard or particle-burst recipes.

stagePlan.name: Render, preserve and troubleshoot
stagePlan.objective: Export verified deliverables, collect all dependencies, compare cold/warm previews and isolate errors systematically.
stagePlan.gate: Render a review and an alpha-capable master, reopen a collected project from another path, and resolve one deliberate failure.
stagePlan.practice: Try the transparent-master and handoff-test recipes.

stagePlan.name: Independent final production
stagePlan.objective: Combine learned skills into an original, reviewable, portable 10-second sequence.
stagePlan.gate: Deliver an independently checked 10-second composition with source files, project backup and an explanation of every major animation choice.
stagePlan.practice: Build the final integrated-sequence recipe without step-by-step imitation.

chapters.title: 01 · Install, identify and prepare AE 25.6
chapters.why: Use the specified 25.6 build on Windows, with a reproducible workspace and no accidental version mismatch.
steps: Open Creative Cloud Desktop on Windows. Locate After Effects and check the installed version through Help → About After Effects. The target is 25.6, not 26.x or a Beta build; available older versions depend on Adobe distribution policies.

Before a large project, confirm the Windows 25.x system requirements: a supported 64-bit Windows release, AVX2-capable CPU, enough RAM, disk space and GPU support. In 25.6, OpenCL 2.0 is required where OpenCL is used; older 1.2 support is discontinued.

Start AE and identify Project, Composition viewer, Timeline, Effect Controls, Effects & Presets, Properties, Preview and Render Queue panels. Hover any panel and tap the backtick key (`) to maximize/restore it.

Choose Window → Workspace, select a standard layout and use Reset to Saved Layout if panels are lost. Use Edit → Preferences to configure auto-save, disk cache and available memory without starving Windows.
Create a dedicated folder such as D:\AE_Learning\01_First_Project. Reserve an Assets subfolder, an Output subfolder and a project backup folder. Avoid relying on temporary Downloads files.
Open Edit → Keyboard Shortcuts (Ctrl+Alt+') to verify bindings on your installed version and keyboard layout. Save a custom preset only if you intentionally change a shortcut.
checks: I can verify 25.6 and locate every central panel.
I have an organized Windows project folder.
I know where the shortcut editor is.
chapters.experiment: Break and restore a workspace layout, then find the Timeline and Effects & Presets in under 30 seconds.
pitfalls: Current Adobe Help pages show 26.x interface features; they are not proof of 25.6 availability.
Do not delete the disk-cache folder while AE is actively writing to it.

chapters.title: 02 · Understand projects, comps, layers and pixels
chapters.why: Build a correct mental model before memorizing commands.
steps: A .aep project is a container of references, compositions, settings and animation; imported images and video normally remain external files. Save Project is not the same as Collect Files or render.

Create a 1920×1080, 24 fps, 8-second composition with Ctrl+N. Name it 01_LAB. Distinguish composition size, frame rate, duration, pixel aspect ratio and background color; the comp background is not automatically an opaque render layer.
Create a blue solid (Ctrl+Y), a text layer (Ctrl+T in an appropriate context), and an empty shape layer (Layer → New → Shape Layer). Stack order determines which pixels cover which in ordinary 2D.
Select the blue layer: P=Position, S=Scale, R=Rotation, T=Opacity, A=Anchor Point. Use Shift+P to add Position while other properties are displayed, and U for animated properties.
Toggle a layer eye, shy, solo, lock, effects (fx), motion blur and 3D switch. Explain how hiding an entire layer differs from bypassing just its effects. F4 changes switches/modes columns.
Learn the vocabulary: footage item vs footage layer, source vs instance, composition vs precomposition, property vs keyframe, mask vs shape, alpha channel vs opacity, effect vs shape operator.
checks: I can describe the project/comp/layer hierarchy.
I can distinguish source items from instances.
I can reveal five transform properties.
chapters.experiment: Duplicate the blue solid layer twice; assign each instance a different Opacity. Observe that all three layers refer to the same Solid Footage source in the Project panel.
pitfalls: Pressing a stopwatch that is already active removes its keyframes.
A background color setting does not add opaque pixels to your output.

chapters.title: 03 · Import and inspect footage correctly
chapters.why: Learn what AE assumes when interpreting each media asset.
steps: Use Ctrl+I to import a PNG with alpha, a JPG, a short constant-frame-rate video, a WAV file and—when available—an image sequence. Check whether the source is a file, sequence or folder.
Double-click footage in Project to open its Footage panel. Compare footage time and frame dimensions with those of your composition. Drag footage into a comp; inspect scaling and frame-rate behavior.
Right-click footage → Interpret Footage → Main. Identify frame rate assumption, field order, pixel aspect ratio and alpha interpretation (straight vs premultiplied); note color options separately.
For an image sequence, select the first frame and use the sequence checkbox only when intended. Verify that frames were numbered without gaps and their order is correct.

Replace a selected layer’s source by Alt-dragging a different source from Project onto the layer. Confirm transform animation and effects remain in place. Distinguish replacing a layer source from replacing a Project item globally.

Make an Assets folder in Project, sort sources and keep originals on disk. If Windows drive letters or source folders change, use Replace Footage to relink the existing Project item; importing the same file again creates a separate item and may leave broken layer references unresolved.
checks: I can interpret footage and verify source frame rates.
I can replace footage without losing a layer animation.
I know where a missing-file reference points.
chapters.experiment: Import a square logo and a wide logo, replace the first with the second using Alt-drag, and observe how the same Scale value affects each.
pitfalls: Variable-frame-rate recordings can cause erratic time or audio sync; use a constant-frame-rate transcode when needed.
Premultiplied alpha interpreted as straight can cause a dark fringe.

chapters.title: 04 · Read time, frames, trims and the work area
chapters.why: The difference between layer time, source time and comp time prevents silent editing errors.
steps: In the Timeline, place the current-time indicator (CTI) at exactly 00:00:02:00 at 24 fps. Use Page Up/Page Down to step frames; Shift+Page Up/Down steps ten frames. Read timecode as hours:minutes:seconds:frames.

Use B and N to set an intentionally short work area. Start/stop Preview with Space; observe the Preview panel options. The work area is a range for preview/render control, not a change to source duration.

With CTI at 1 second, select a footage layer and press [ to shift its entire layer bar so the In point meets CTI. Next move CTI to 2 seconds, press Alt+[ to trim the In point without moving the entire layer. Undo twice and compare layer Start Time, In point and source frames.
Use Alt+] to trim the out point, Ctrl+Shift+D to split, Ctrl+D to duplicate, and I/O to jump to a selected layer’s in/out points. Practice knowing which commands change the source span.
Move the Timeline zoom using = / - on the main keyboard. Toggle full-span/single-frame viewing with ;. View one exact source frame, then locate it after shifting the layer.
Set marker(s) to plan beats. A composition marker differs from a layer marker; both differ from a keyframe. Save an experiment copy before drastic trimming.
checks: I can step to a specific frame.
I know the distinction between moving, trimming and splitting.
I can define a work area.
chapters.experiment: Build a 4-second card transition that changes from a blue card to a red card at exactly 48 frames.
pitfalls: At 24 fps, :23 is the last frame within a numbered second; :24 is not an in-second frame.
The main keyboard 0 and numpad 0 may do different things.

chapters.title: 05 · Anchor, Position, Scale and parenting
chapters.why: Spatial transforms are predictable once you understand coordinate spaces.
steps: Draw a 200×200 rectangle in a Shape Layer. Press P to inspect the comp-space Position of the shape layer’s anchor; press A to inspect its layer-space Anchor Point (which may not coincide with the rectangle’s own group center). Changing one is not the same as changing the other.

Move the anchor with the Pan Behind tool (Y). Rotate with R; notice where rotation occurs. To center the anchor within content, test Ctrl+Alt+Home and compare the result with Ctrl+Home, which centers the layer’s anchor in the comp.
Create a Null Object (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y). Parent the shape and text to the null using the Parent & Link pick whip. Move, scale and rotate the null; then inspect each child’s local transform.
Unparent one child and watch its on-screen pose if AE compensates its transform. Explain why parenting does not mean copying Position keyframes or merging layers.
For a 3D layer, Position has three dimensions and rotation/orientation differs from the 2D case. Do not introduce a camera yet; use the 3D switch only for a controlled experiment.
Build a single controller named CTRL_RIG, and do not put unrelated effects on it. Label layers clearly and lock controllers when their position is correct.
checks: I can tell anchor and position apart.
I can parent two layers to a null.
I can explain local vs comp coordinates.
chapters.experiment: Animate the null in a circle while rotating an independently animated child around its own pivot.
pitfalls: Changing a child parent can alter coordinate interpretation.
Centering a layer and centering its anchor are different commands.

chapters.title: 06 · Create and remove keyframes safely
chapters.why: Animate one number correctly before adding complex rigs.
steps: Add a Position keyframe at time 0 by clicking the stopwatch once. Move to 1 second and drag the object to a new Position. Inspect the two diamonds in the Timeline.

Return to time 0, reveal Opacity with T, set it to 100 and click its stopwatch to create the first Opacity keyframe. Then move to 2 seconds and change Opacity to 0 to create the second key. Without that first keyframe, the change at 2 seconds would simply set a constant value rather than a fade.

Select only one keyframe and press Delete. Rebuild it. To remove all Position keys, click the active stopwatch: observe that every keyframe vanishes and the current value is retained. Undo immediately.
Use U to show only animated properties, UU to show all properties modified from defaults, and K/J to jump visible keyframes/markers.
Use Alt+Shift+P or Alt+Shift+T to add/remove a key at CTI on the appropriate property; this does not toggle the whole property’s animation stopwatch.
Copy two selected Position keyframes, place CTI elsewhere and paste. Note that the first pasted key usually aligns with CTI. Use a separate duplicate layer to compare variations.
checks: I can create, move and remove a single keyframe.
I understand the dangerous stopwatch toggle.
I can show only animated properties.
chapters.experiment: Animate a circle from x=200 to x=1720 in exactly 2 seconds, then fade it in for the first 12 frames.
pitfalls: Auto-keyframing can enable animation for new properties automatically; leave it off while learning.
Deleting one key is not the same as deactivating the stopwatch.

chapters.title: 07 · Design motion with the Graph Editor
chapters.why: Good animation depends on velocity and spacing, not just destinations.
steps: Create Position keyframes 0 and 1 second, 800 pixels apart. Set both Linear, preview, and notice constant perceived speed on a straight path.

Select both keys and press F9 (Easy Ease). Use Shift+F3 to open the Graph Editor. Locate Speed Graph and Value Graph modes; for Position, choosing Separate Dimensions changes the way you can edit curves.
In Speed Graph, make the object accelerate quickly and decelerate gently. Preview and compare. Inspect motion-path dots: dense dots represent smaller distance per sample and hence slower motion.
Make a third middle Position key; separate spatial path curvature (trajectory) from the time interpolation (velocity). A curved path can move at constant speed, and a straight path can ease.
Use Easy Ease In/Out intentionally. For a stepped stop-motion look, test Toggle Hold Keyframe. Observe that Hold is not the same as a slow Bézier curve.
Open Keyframe Velocity (Ctrl+Shift+K) when numerical influence is necessary. Save a tiny file containing three clearly named easing examples.
checks: I can explain speed vs value graphs.
I can make linear, eased and hold movement.
I understand spatial vs temporal curves.
chapters.experiment: Make three identical circles travel 500 px with linear, ease-out and overshoot movement; render a side-by-side comparison.
pitfalls: Tweaking spatial Bézier handles changes the path rather than temporal easing.
Position Separate Dimensions removes the unified motion path representation.

chapters.title: 08 · Draw shapes and parametric shape operators
chapters.why: Distinguish vector geometry, paths, styles and per-group transformations.
steps: Deselect all layers and use Q to draw a rectangle. It creates a Shape Layer. Expand Contents → Rectangle → Rectangle Path, Fill, Stroke, and the shape group’s Transform; compare with the layer’s separate Transform group.
Make an Ellipse and a Polystar with the Q tool cycle. Change parametric Size, Roundness, Points and radii. Do not convert to Bézier until you actually need manual vertices.
Use Contents → Add → Trim Paths and animate End from 0 to 100 on a stroked path. Set Start and Offset to explore moving a dash around a loop.
Use Repeater to create repeated copies of a group. Find Copies, Offset and Transform: Repeater → Position, Rotation, Scale. Explain why changing original geometry affects every repeated instance.
Explore Offset Paths, Pucker & Bloat, Zig Zag, Twist and Wiggle Paths one at a time. Turn each operator off and on to isolate its effect.
Convert a duplicated parametric path to Bézier; move a vertex with Pen/Selection tools. Try a closed filled shape and an open stroked path to compare filling behavior.
checks: I can locate group Transform vs layer Transform.
I can animate Trim Paths and Repeater.
I can choose parametric vs Bézier geometry.
chapters.experiment: Make a rotating loading indicator consisting of twelve repeated ticks and a Trim Paths ring.
pitfalls: An empty Shape Layer has no visible pixels.
Shape operators are not in the Effect Controls effects list.

chapters.title: 09 · Understand masks and alpha
chapters.why: Transparency has several independent sources, each suited to different work.
steps: Add a photograph to a comp. Select the photograph and draw a rectangle: it normally creates a mask on the selected layer. Deselect and draw another rectangle: it creates a shape layer. Check the toolbar mask/shape mode.
Press MM to reveal mask groups. For each mask test Mode Add, Subtract, Intersect and None, then change Feather, Expansion and Opacity and invert the mask.
Animate Mask Path over several frames to follow a moving subject. Make simple wide shapes first; excessive vertices are harder to stabilize and maintain.
Set a high feather value, then change layer Opacity separately. Inspect the Alpha channel via Alt+4. A transparent pixel can still have RGB values; alpha determines coverage.
Draw two masks on the same layer; test which mode is used and whether the order changes results. Enable/disable masks independently without deleting their path keys.
Precompose masked imagery and compare the look with and without Collapse Transformations in a controlled vector/precomp case; do not assume the switch is a free quality upgrade.
checks: I can create a mask on a selected layer.
I can adjust feather, expansion and modes.
I can inspect actual alpha separately.
chapters.experiment: Cut a circular window into a photo and animate the window to follow a bouncing ball.
pitfalls: An animated mask is not a motion-tracked mask until you track it.
High feather is not a cure for poor matte edges.

chapters.title: 10 · Use track mattes and blend modes
chapters.why: Mattes let one layer control visibility of another without drawing directly on the target.
steps: Create a text layer above a video layer. In the video layer’s TrkMat column select the text layer as its matte source. Modern AE track mattes can refer to another layer without that matte being directly above the target.
Test Alpha Matte versus Alpha Inverted Matte. Then use a luminance gradient and select Luma Matte versus Luma Inverted Matte. Identify what white, black and grey mean in each mode.
Try a transparent red-to-blue shape as a matte and inspect why its alpha can be constant although its luminance varies dramatically. Convert to grayscale for a predictable luma test.
Use F4 to reveal Switches/Modes where necessary. Compare Normal, Multiply, Screen, Add and Overlay on the same footage with two test layers.
Precompose only when the matte has to become a reusable source or when an effect must operate after the matte. A simple matte relationship does not automatically require a precomp.
Render to a format supporting alpha and verify transparency over a checkerboard outside AE. A matte preview on black is not proof that alpha was exported.
checks: I can choose alpha vs luma matte.
I can invert either matte.
I can demonstrate an actual transparent export.
chapters.experiment: Make a 3-second title reveal in which video is visible only inside moving letters.
pitfalls: Screen blend mode against black does not create real alpha.
Layer opacity and track-matte coverage multiply in the final composite.

chapters.title: 11 · Precompositions, nested time and render order
chapters.why: Precomps organize work, but also change which operations happen first.
steps: Select three animated layers and precompose with Ctrl+Shift+C. Name the new comp 02_ICON_UNIT; with multiple selected layers After Effects uses Move all attributes into the new composition. To compare with Leave all attributes, make a separate single-layer footage/solid test (not a shape or text layer), precompose it, and inspect both dialog choices.
Open the precomp and note the inner time, duration, and layer layout. Return to the master comp and alter the precomp layer transform. Inspect whether the inner animation still plays as intended.

Apply Gaussian Blur to a shape, then precompose with different attribute settings; compare effect-before-transform with effect-after-transform. Render order is the reason precomposing can change an effect’s appearance.
In a duplicated test comp, toggle Collapse Transformations on the nested comp. Observe changed transformations, masks, 3D interactions and effect results rather than universally enabling the switch.
Use Time Remapping and an Essential Property only after the nested comp behaves consistently. Name instances uniquely when they need different controls.
Add a short marker on master comp corresponding to a specific event inside the precomp. Document any shifted inner start times and audio synchronization.
checks: I can precompose with an intentional attribute choice.
I can explain a changed blur after precomposition.
I can locate inner vs outer time.
chapters.experiment: Build a lower-third as its own comp, duplicate it twice in a master comp and vary scale/timing without editing the internal artwork.
pitfalls: Collapse Transformations is not a generic quality switch.
Precompose can change how adjustment layers, 3D and effects interact.

chapters.title: 12 · Typography and animated text selectors
chapters.why: Type in motion is a system of characters, paragraphs, layout and animation selectors.
steps: Use Ctrl+T to create point text with a click and paragraph text by dragging a text box. Test different wrapping, alignment, font weight and paragraph settings in Character/Paragraph.
Make two headings with consistent font family and sizes; use tracking and leading intentionally. Use native text rather than rasterizing type when you need accessibility and later wording changes.
Expand Text → Animate → Position and add an Opacity animator. Open Range Selector → Advanced; compare Based On Characters, Characters Excluding Spaces, Words and Lines.
Animate Range Selector Offset from -100% to 100% to sweep a reveal. Compare Smoothness 0 to 100 and different selector shapes for stepped vs continuous entrances.
Use Text → Path Options when appropriate to put characters along a mask path. A text-on-path system is different from converting text to outlines.
Create two text layers, apply only a few font and style changes, and test 25.4+ copy/paste text formatting where available. Verify the paste action in the text editing context.
checks: I can distinguish point and paragraph text.
I can animate words and letters separately.
I can use Range Selector Offset.
chapters.experiment: Make a 5-second kinetic typography card with per-word emphasis, clean baseline and a safe screen margin.
pitfalls: Per-character expressions added in 25.0 are different from variable-font axis animation introduced in 26.0.
Using the same keybindings while editing text can trigger text editing commands instead of layer shortcuts.

chapters.title: 13 · Learn effects, order and adjustment layers
chapters.why: Effects compute images in sequence, and the order is part of the design.
steps: Create a solid with Fractal Noise; apply Levels, Tint, Turbulent Displace and Glow in that order. Duplicate the layer and reorder Glow before Levels. Compare the different result.

Open Effect Controls with F3. Rename each effect instance by its purpose. Toggle its fx switch; note that disabling an effect is nondestructive while Ctrl+Shift+E removes all effects from selected layers.
Make an Adjustment Layer (Ctrl+Alt+Y) and apply Curves. Put it above two footage layers; toggle layer order and note which lower pixels it modifies.
Compare an effect applied to a footage layer, the same effect on a precomp, and an effect on an adjustment layer. They do not use identical inputs in all cases.

Open the Effect Manager if a plugin appears missing or disabled. Use Effects & Presets search rather than assuming every installed effect has an application-wide search launcher; Quick Apply (Ctrl+Enter) is 26.2, not 25.6.
Test effect compatibility at 8, 16 and 32 bpc in Project Settings. An effect may process fewer bit depths or be CPU-only; check supported modes for the actual installed 25.6 effect.
checks: I can rearrange effects to change render results.
I understand adjustment layers.
I can distinguish bypass from deletion.
chapters.experiment: Build a cloudy glow effect with at least four effects; save an Animation Preset for reuse.
pitfalls: Effects & Presets search is not the 26.2 Quick Apply launcher.
An effect called a 3D effect does not necessarily create an actual 3D layer.

chapters.title: 14 · Blur, glow, noise and depth maps
chapters.why: Understand the purpose of blur and procedural textures instead of applying random presets.
steps: Place Gaussian Blur on a photographic layer. Increase Blurriness and compare Repeat Edge Pixels on/off around the boundaries.
On a duplicate, use Camera Lens Blur and configure lens properties. Compare computational cost and appearance with a Gaussian Blur of similar apparent radius.
Generate a grayscale Fractal Noise texture on another layer. Use Displacement Map to warp a checkerboard; inspect map source channel, Max Horizontal/Vertical Displacement and map resolution.
Try Compound Blur or Camera Lens Blur with a blur/depth map and feathered transitions. A depth map controls *where* blurring occurs; it is not the same as overall lens bokeh settings.

Make a glow source by isolating bright pixels through Levels, then apply Glow with intentional Threshold, Radius and Intensity. Note why adding glow to a full-bright white rectangle washes out the whole scene.
Animate Fractal Noise Evolution and Offset Turbulence. Use it as a texture, matte, displacement driver or blend overlay, checking noise aliasing at final resolution.
checks: I can choose ordinary vs lens-like blur.
I can use a grayscale map to deform or blur.
I can keep a glow controllable.
chapters.experiment: Build a heat-haze transition using Fractal Noise as an animated Displacement Map.
pitfalls: 26.3 Curl Noise is not present in 25.6.
Too much glow can destroy edge contrast and alpha quality.

chapters.title: 15 · Time remap, speed, loops and motion blur
chapters.why: Temporal sampling affects motion even when no transform changes.
steps: Put a clip in a comp. Compare Time Stretch, Time-Reverse Layer (Ctrl+Alt+R), and Time Remapping (Ctrl+Alt+T). Record which changes source speed and which changes the timing of layer keyframes.
Enable Time Remapping on a duplicate and add a middle keyframe to speed up one segment and slow down another. Inspect interpolation: smooth time remapping can freeze or reverse segments.
For looping source playback, locate the final valid source frame and the default end-time key. Remove or adjust the problematic end key before adding loopOut('cycle') to Time Remap if required.
Use Posterize Time on a duplicate to create a stepped frame-rate aesthetic. Distinguish it from changing the *composition* frame rate.
Animate a fast-moving shape. Toggle its Motion Blur switch and the comp’s master Motion Blur switch. Adjust shutter angle and shutter phase under comp Advanced settings; judge at full speed.
Compare native motion blur with CC Force Motion Blur or Pixel Motion Blur where available. Third-party/plugins and frame interpolation may need substantially more rendering time.
checks: I can reverse footage and remap it.
I can loop without an extra flash at the seam.
I can enable both motion blur switches.
chapters.experiment: Create three 2-second strips: smooth moving circle, 12-fps posterized circle and motion-blurred circle.
pitfalls: Motion blur is not added just because a layer has Position keyframes.
Time Remap source duration endpoints can be off by one visible frame.

chapters.title: 16 · Audio levels, waveform and reactive graphics
chapters.why: AE can synchronize and drive animation from audio, but is not a full DAW.
steps: Import a WAV with predictable beats. Press L for Audio Levels and LL (two quick taps) for its waveform; use numpad decimal for audio-only preview on a standard keyboard.
Set clear timeline markers at beats. Trim and reposition sound without accidentally offsetting its start relative to animated elements; use the Info panel if needed.
Select audio → Animation → Keyframe Assistant → Convert Audio to Keyframes. Inspect the resulting Audio Amplitude null and Both Channels Slider keyframes.
On a shape’s Scale, Alt+click the stopwatch and use a simple expression driven by the slider. For example: a=thisComp.layer('Audio Amplitude').effect('Both Channels')('Slider'); [100+a*2,100+a*2];.
Smooth noisy values with the smooth() expression when needed or keyframe smoothing, and clamp extreme peaks. Build a minimum scale so silence does not collapse the graphic.
Export a preview and listen to it. Audio playback from the computer can differ from a final encoded render; check that audio output is explicitly enabled in the Output Module.
checks: I can reveal an audio waveform.
I can convert audio to control keys.
I can make a shape pulse to audio.
chapters.experiment: Animate a 5-bar equalizer-like display using five linked or differently remapped audio amplitude values.
pitfalls: Audio amplitude generated by the assistant is a numerical representation, not a beat classifier.
An audio effect can modify the sound, not just a visible waveform.

chapters.title: 17 · Green/blue-screen compositing
chapters.why: Professional keying separates core opacity, edge detail and spill removal.
steps: Import evenly lit green-screen footage. Put a contrasting background beneath it, then apply Keylight (1.2) to the footage.
Pick a representative green Screen Colour away from hair/skin. Switch Keylight View to Screen Matte. Adjust Clip Black and Clip White moderately to establish opaque subject and clean background.
Inspect fine hair and semi-transparent material. Use Screen Shrink/Grow and Screen Softness carefully; extreme crushing loses legitimate edge detail.
Add Key Cleaner and Advanced Spill Suppressor after Keylight when useful. Compare suppression modes and check green reflections in grey or skin regions.

Use a garbage mask to eliminate off-screen gear and nonuniform regions before or alongside keying. Use separate inside and edge mattes for challenging footage rather than forcing one setting for every region.
Check the keyed subject against black, white, saturated grey and final intended background. Add light wrap/grade if visually needed, but keep a clean premultiplied edge.
checks: I can read the Keylight screen matte.
I can distinguish matte cleanup from spill suppression.
I can inspect alpha on four backgrounds.
chapters.experiment: Produce a 5-second talking-head composite against a still photograph, with stable hair edges.
pitfalls: Cranking Clip Black/White removes real fine detail.
Luma matte does not automatically replace chroma keying.

chapters.title: 18 · Track a moving point and stabilize motion
chapters.why: Tracking turns observations in footage into reusable transformations.
steps: Select a footage layer and open Window → Tracker. Choose Track Motion. Start with a high-contrast feature that does not rotate out of view; define Feature and Search Regions.
Track forward in small portions and inspect drift. Set the Attach Point thoughtfully; the feature region may move while the attachment stays separately positioned.
Create a Null, set Edit Target to that Null, and Apply the tracking data. Parent a graphic to the null rather than pasting tracking keys into every child.
Enable rotation and scale tracking by using two tracking points when the footage supports stable features. Know that point trackers cannot inherently solve full perspective deformation.
Use Stabilize Motion on a duplicate; note how the image edges move and why you may need scaling/cropping or synthesis for blank edges.

For planar surfaces and perspective replacement, open bundled Mocha AE, track a plane, then send corner-pin data back into AE. Verify the exact Mocha integration commands in the installed plugin version.
checks: I can apply a point track to a Null.
I can detect and repair track drift.
I can distinguish point tracking from planar tracking.
chapters.experiment: Track a moving label onto a high-contrast point on a recorded object for 3 seconds.
pitfalls: A successful tracker preview can still drift after an occlusion.
Warp Stabilizer is not a simple replacement for perspective planar tracking.

chapters.title: 19 · Roto Brush, Refine Edge and mask tracking
chapters.why: Extract moving subjects without the 2026 Object Matte feature.
steps: Duplicate a video layer and open that layer in the Layer panel, not only the Composition panel. Activate Roto Brush (Alt+W) and create foreground strokes where the intended subject has recognizable edges.
Use Alt with the brush, where supported, to subtract incorrectly selected regions. Identify the base frame and propagate forward/backward through a manageable span.
Scrub the full span and repair frames that drift, especially fast-moving hands, occlusions and hair. Use Refine Edge on semitransparent detail only after the main segmentation is stable.

Adjust Reduce Chatter, Feather, Shift Edge and Decontaminate Edge Colors as warranted, then Freeze propagation for the span. Keep the source footage available; Freeze is not the same as rendering a permanent matte file.
Use Mask Tracking on an appropriately drawn mask for rigid, easy-to-follow objects. If motion is complex, consider manual correction or a separate point/planar track.
Pre-render a clean RGBA intermediate when editing further becomes slow; verify that the output format actually retains an alpha channel.
checks: I can roto a 2-second moving subject.
I understand propagation and Freeze.
I can choose mask tracking vs Roto Brush.
chapters.experiment: Cut a person out of an indoor clip and place a moving procedural texture behind the subject.
pitfalls: Object Matte was introduced in After Effects 26.2, so 25.6 uses Roto Brush/Refine Edge/Mask Tracking instead.
Freezing a roto span does not replace checking every frame.

chapters.title: 20 · Paint, clone and Content-Aware Fill
chapters.why: Moving from an obvious brush stroke to credible invisible repair requires temporal checking.
steps: Double-click footage to work in the Layer panel. Use Brush, Clone Stamp and Eraser there; the same tool is not just a normal Comp-view shape brush.
Set a Clone Stamp sampling point with Alt+click. Paint a small patch on a duplicate and test source alignment and stroke duration modes in the Paint panel.
Make a simple repair with painting, then preview over time. A correction that matches one frame can slide or flicker after motion unless properly tracked or the paint is adjusted.
Use a mask around an unwanted object, follow it with keyframes or tracking, and open Window → Content-Aware Fill. Select the appropriate Fill Method and Range, then Generate Fill Layer.

For a difficult frame, create a reference frame in Photoshop (when available) or a suitable still-image editor; fill the defect and return the reference to AE. Manage source paths and regenerated fills.
Evaluate repeated textures, camera motion, shadows and occlusion. Sometimes a clean plate plus planar tracking is more reliable than automated Fill.
checks: I can clone a small detail.
I can generate a Content-Aware Fill layer.
I know when to use a tracked clean plate.
chapters.experiment: Remove a small stationary sticker from a 2-second shot with a moving handheld camera.
pitfalls: Brush/Clone Stamp stroke duration matters.
Content-Aware Fill may hallucinate repetition or change a texture over time.

chapters.title: 21 · 2.5D parallax, cameras and lights
chapters.why: AE 3D layers exist in 3D space, but not every 3D-looking effect behaves as scene geometry.
steps: Turn on 3D switches for several photos or shape layers and separate them in Z depth. Create a Camera (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+C). Distinguish 1-node and 2-node camera behavior, point of interest, zoom and field of view.

Create a Camera orbit Null and parent the camera to it for controlled moves, or animate camera Position/Point Of Interest intentionally. Use multiple views to check that foreground and background have the desired depth separation.
Add a Light (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+L) and test Material Options on 3D layers. Understand Accepts Lights/Shadows and limitations of the selected 3D renderer.
Switch Project Settings/Composition Advanced 3D renderer only intentionally; Classic 3D, Cinema 4D and Advanced 3D do not have identical feature sets. Test native 3D models where supported.
In After Effects 25.6, select multiple 3D layers to use the shared/single 3D transform gizmo; also inspect View → Default Camera Settings for the new default camera controls.

For camera depth-of-field needs, verify the chosen renderer. 26.3 added in-engine Advanced 3D Depth of Field; do not confuse that newer feature with older camera DOF workflows in other renderers or 2D lens-blur simulations.
checks: I can make a 3-layer parallax scene.
I can distinguish renderers and camera types.
I can locate 25.6 shared gizmo controls.
chapters.experiment: Create a 6-second dolly move through three cut-out images at different Z positions, avoiding obvious image edges.
pitfalls: 2D effects like CC Sphere or 3D Channel effects do not become scene geometry by naming alone.
Advanced 3D renderer feature support differs from Classic 3D.

chapters.title: 22 · Camera tracking and screen replacement
chapters.why: Choose a scene-solving tool based on camera motion rather than the look of the final effect.
steps: Use a shot with real parallax: camera moves through a room rather than only rotating from one point. Apply 3D Camera Tracker and allow Analysis/Solving to finish.
Inspect the track points and locate a plausible horizontal plane. Target a triad and create a Solid/Camera or Text/Camera. Check the solved graphic over all frames, not only the initial one.
If the solve is unstable, inspect fast pans, rolling shutter, motion blur, zoom changes, focal length and low-parallax shots. Trim and stabilize the analysis source where justified.
For a planar phone screen, compare Mocha AE corner pin or built-in perspective tracker. Use a high-contrast planar patch, not an assumption that a 3D camera solve will always be superior.
Track a sign or poster, then apply Corner Pin/CC Power Pin to the replacement screen. Control the insert’s color, noise and motion blur to match the plate.
Export a diagnostic video showing the tracker points or a checkerboard overlaid on the final surface; a drifting corner is easier to catch with a grid than with a textured replacement.
checks: I can solve a simple parallax clip.
I can choose a planar track for a screen.
I can check perspective replacement on every frame.
chapters.experiment: Replace a moving phone screen with a checkerboard, then with a custom animated interface.
pitfalls: 3D Camera Tracker will not solve every low-parallax or heavily blurred clip.
Screen corner tracking is not equivalent to full-scene camera recovery.

chapters.title: 23 · Color correction, working space and alpha
chapters.why: Correct color requires keeping separate input interpretation, working-space math, display, and output.
steps: In File → Project Settings → Color, compare color-managed versus unmanaged workflows in a small 8/16/32-bpc experiment. Choose an intentional Working Color Space for the target delivery.

Inspect an imported image’s Interpret Footage color settings. When necessary, assign the right input profile; assigning a profile changes interpretation and is not the same thing as changing RGB values with an effect.
Use Lumetri Color, Curves and Levels on a test image. Correct exposure/contrast/white balance first, then make a look. View histograms or scopes where available and compare to a controlled reference.
Understand straight vs premultiplied alpha and RGB in transparent pixels. Remove Color Matting when necessary; a matte halo is not always fixed by globally sharpening an image.

For an OCIO/ACES workflow, select a known supported configuration, interpret input color spaces, preview through a chosen view transform, and set intended output transform. Do not claim native bundled ACES 2.0 configs in 25.6; those arrive in 26.5.
Export a tagged test image/video and compare the rendered file in a color-managed viewer. Different Windows video apps may apply different display transforms; check metadata, not just eye judgment.
checks: I know input vs working vs display vs output space.
I can explain 8/16/32 bpc.
I can test alpha against light/dark backgrounds.
chapters.experiment: Grade the same PNG to neutral in an 8-bpc unmanaged project and a 16-bpc color-managed project; document the differences.
pitfalls: Increasing bpc does not restore clipped source data.
Do not use an ACES 2.0 feature added in 26.5 as a 25.6 instruction.

chapters.title: 24 · Expressions: build a repeatable controller
chapters.why: Expressions compute property values; learn safe interfaces before writing complex JavaScript.
steps: Create a Null named CTRL. Apply Effect → Expression Controls → Slider Control, rename it Speed. On another layer’s Rotation, Alt+click its stopwatch once and enter time*thisComp.layer('CTRL').effect('Speed')('Slider');.
Set Speed to 0, 90 and -45; verify that the graphic stops, rotates clockwise and counterclockwise. Your expression needs a numeric output because Rotation expects a scalar.
On a 2D Position property, enter wiggle(1,20); and compare with value+[Math.sin(time*2)*20,0];. Distinguish nondeterministic-looking wiggle from smooth periodic motion.
Make a 2D Scale expression using [100,100] or [s,s], not a lone scalar. Learn value, time, thisComp, thisLayer, framesToTime(), ease(), linear(), clamp(), loopOut().
Create two expression-linked layers using the pick whip rather than manually typing names, then rename a controller and inspect references. Handle missing effects or source layer changes carefully.
Toggle an expression off without deleting it. Use Animation → Keyframe Assistant → Convert Expression to Keyframes to bake a copy when needed for portability or delivery.
checks: I can create a slider-controlled rotation.
I can return the correct value dimension.
I can disable vs delete an expression.
chapters.experiment: Build one Null with Speed, Amount and Color Control driving a three-layer animated indicator.
pitfalls: Expressions are not general browser JavaScript; DOM/HTML APIs are unavailable.
An expression controller can introduce a fragile dependency on its layer name.

chapters.title: 25 · Data-driven text and graphics
chapters.why: Separate content from animation so recurring work is faster to update.
steps: Create a small UTF-8 CSV or TSV with name, score and color columns. Import it as data through File → Import and inspect its accessible data properties.
Use expression pick whipping or the available footage data methods to read row values. Start with literal values before adding a drop-down selector or a row index slider.
Create a Score text layer and set Source Text from a suitable string expression. Format numbers deliberately with Math.round(), toFixed() or String() where appropriate.
Build a background rectangle sized to text with sourceRectAtTime(); add horizontal and vertical padding, and inspect left/top offsets to avoid misalignment.
Try importing a small JSON object as footage and reading a nested key by expression using footage('filename.json').sourceData. Keep field names stable and check for missing keys.
Make a reusable template with editable content and named controls. Document what changes without touching timeline keys.
checks: I can import one data file.
I can link text to a value.
I can keep animated layout working after the string changes.
chapters.experiment: Make a three-slide statistics board generated from a CSV, each with an auto-sized number card.
pitfalls: Imported data schema paths are easy to misaddress: inspect the data structure.
SourceText may contain formatted objects; test with the target 25.6 expression engine.

chapters.title: 26 · Essential Properties and MOGRT delivery
chapters.why: Build assets that another editor can adjust without breaking a controlled design.
steps: Create a child comp containing a title, subtitle, color plate and simple entrance animation. Open Window → Essential Graphics and select the correct master composition.
Expose editable Source Text, key color controls and a Slider into Essential Graphics. Rename controls clearly, group when appropriate and provide default values.
Nest the child comp twice; inspect Essential Properties for each instance. Change one instance’s title and color while retaining the original child comp and other instance.
Test protected regions for intro/outro timing when building a reusable MOGRT, then stretch a middle region in a deliberately long test comp. Check that animation does not overlap unexpectedly.
Export a Motion Graphics Template (.mogrt) and choose the correct destination; use a video preview where supported. Verify third-party fonts/plugins or expression dependencies.
Open or install the MOGRT in a compatible Adobe workflow where available; test exposed controls, resolution and duration. Retain the original .aep and assets as source of truth.
checks: I can expose one editable text property.
I can customize two comp instances.
I know the distinction between a .mogrt and an .aep.
chapters.experiment: Make a lower-third MOGRT with name, role, primary color and adjustable hold duration.
pitfalls: MOGRT export cannot magically package every third-party dependency.
Essential Properties are instance overrides, not a replacement for all original animation data.

chapters.title: 27 · Native 3D models, environments and renderers
chapters.why: Use only the mesh and model capabilities actually available in AE 25.6.
steps: Import a supported 3D model format available to 25.6, including supported GLB/GLTF/OBJ or FBX as applicable to your project/build. Inspect scale, axes, texture material paths and animation playback.
Create a 3D composition using the Advanced 3D renderer. Add an environment light or HDRI for reflections and test an animated environment light (introduced in 25.2).
Check each model’s Material Options, Accepts Lights, Shadows and shadow-catcher workflow. Compare quality/performance options and confirm the actual render, not only Fast Draft.
Use the shared single 3D gizmo on multiple selected 3D layers (25.6 feature) to transform as a group visually. Learn that it changes individual layers; it is not necessarily a persistent parent rig.
Change View → Default Camera Settings (25.6) to adjust the way default/custom views behave. Save a test and inspect composition views before and after.
For geometric primitives, create shapes or use an imported mesh asset. Direct native parametric 3D mesh creation and Substance 3D material support belong to 26.0+, not this manual’s target.
checks: I can import one model and light it.
I can test an environment light.
I can identify two 3D features new in 25.6.
chapters.experiment: Build an 8-second product turntable using a supported 3D model and a controlled camera orbit.
pitfalls: 3D model and material import support varies by format/renderer.
Native parametric mesh creation is not a 25.6 feature.

chapters.title: 28 · Puppet rigging and deformation
chapters.why: Animate flexible artwork without cutting it into dozens of rigid pieces.
steps: Import a transparent character or ribbon. Duplicate the source and apply Puppet pins to a clean alpha layer while in the relevant Puppet tool mode.
Add pins to stable regions first: base/shoulder, elbow and tip. Move a single pin over time and inspect how the mesh deforms between pins.
Explore Overlap and Starch tools to control drawing order and rigidity in supported Puppet modes. Place pins where the mesh should bend and where it should resist stretching.
Reduce pin counts until you can understand every pin. An over-constrained mesh creates awkward hard bends or almost no visible motion.
Precompose when the Puppet effect needs to move with a separate rigid transform. Compare deform-then-scale with scale-then-deform in your hierarchy.
Render a seamless 2-second loop; inspect pin intersections and anti-aliased alpha edges at every extreme.
checks: I can make a simple Puppet mesh.
I can set stiffness/overlap deliberately.
I can animate a clean loop.
chapters.experiment: Make a waving flag or cartoon arm bend while its base remains fixed.
pitfalls: Puppet is a deformation tool, not skeletal 3D rigging by itself.
Tiny transparent holes can distort a mesh unexpectedly.

chapters.title: 29 · Native particle and simulation systems
chapters.why: Learn particle emitters, lifetimes and physics controls through measurable experiments.
steps: Apply CC Particle World to a solid. Find Producer Position and Radius, Birth Rate, Longevity, Particle Type, Velocity, Gravity and Resistance controls.

Set Birth Rate low and Longevity short. Measure how many visible particles appear at once; rough steady count depends on rate × lifetime, though frame integration and fade settings affect the rendered result.
Make a second particle system using CC Particle Systems II. Compare available controls and rendering performance instead of assuming both systems are interchangeable.
Try CC Rainfall or CC Snowfall and then Foam or CC Bubbles. Understand emitter-based versus image-distortion-based animation.
Precompose particle sources when layering glow, blur and mattes. Test whether effect order changes source/particle size or the glow of particles.
Make a 5-second rain field that respects foreground occlusion via track matte and includes variation in size, velocity and blur.
checks: I can control birth rate and lifetime.
I can compare native particle tools.
I can matte particles behind an object.
chapters.experiment: Create a burst that emits for 12 frames, falls under gravity and fades within 3 seconds.
pitfalls: Particle count is not simply Birth Rate without accounting for particle lifetime.
Some CC effects expose controls in normalized coordinates, not comp pixels.

chapters.title: 30 · ExtendScript, scripts and batch workflow
chapters.why: Understand which tasks need property expressions and which need application automation.
steps: Distinguish expressions (a formula on a property, evaluated over time) from ExtendScript/JSX scripts (commands that build or edit project objects). A regular expression cannot import and rename 200 files or create arbitrary layers.
Learn the project object model at a high level: app.project, items, compositions, layers, properties, keyframes, and render queue items. Keep automation scripts narrowly scoped.

Create a reversible experiment: a simple JSX script run through File → Scripts → Run Script File that makes a named solid and saves no files automatically. Review permissions/prefs relevant to scripts before running.
Use undo groups around edits and test on a copy. Always guard the selected item type and active composition before dereferencing it.
For external data, prefer explicit JSON/CSV inputs, deterministic naming and a record of generated assets. Do not put sensitive information inside easily shared project expressions.
Try a batch task such as renaming layers with a prefix or setting comp frame rates only after manually checking the intended targets. Compare before/after project structure.
checks: I can distinguish JSX scripts from expressions.
I can describe project item vs layer objects.
I can test scripts safely on a copy.
chapters.experiment: Write a short JSX script that enumerates comp names and reports them, without changing the project.
pitfalls: Scripts can alter a project or access files; only run code you understand and trust.
An expression’s JavaScript support is not the same as a script’s API.

chapters.title: 31 · Render Queue, codecs, alpha and audio
chapters.why: Choose the output to match its downstream use and verify what the render actually contains.
steps: Save your project. Select the final composition and use Ctrl+Shift+/ to add it to Render Queue. Inspect Render Settings, Output Module, and Output To separately.

Set a working review output, such as an H.264 MP4 where the installed 25.6 encoder and selected output route support it. Alternatively queue an Adobe Media Encoder output using Ctrl+Alt+M. Do not rely on one codec for every delivery.
For a master or intermediate, choose a high-quality suitable codec such as ProRes or DNxHR (where available), or an image sequence. Specify bit depth, frame rate, color tagging and audio as intended.

For transparency, use a format/codecs that support alpha, select RGB+Alpha, and specify Straight or Premultiplied according to downstream requirements. Standard H.264 MP4 generally does not carry normal AE RGBA transparency.
Render only intended work area or entire comp explicitly. Check that the final frame, 100% resolution, high-quality sampling and motion blur correspond to your delivery requirements.
Open the rendered output in a separate player/editor. Count frames, inspect audio sync, color, alpha and first/last frame. A successful Render Queue status does not certify the file is correct.
checks: I can export a review movie and an RGBA master.
I can distinguish render settings vs output module.
I can inspect a render externally.
chapters.experiment: Deliver one MP4 review, one transparent master or PNG sequence, and a written export checklist.
pitfalls: Choosing RGB+Alpha does nothing if the selected codec/container cannot carry an alpha channel.
Rendered H.264 export is not the same as saving an editable project.

chapters.title: 32 · Backups, Collect Files and team handoff
chapters.why: Keep a project reproducible after assets move or the original editor is unavailable.
steps: Save the working .aep, then use File → Dependencies → Collect Files to gather used sources into a package. Read the available options and select a dedicated collection folder.
Relocate/copy the collected folder to a different Windows path or drive letter, open the collected .aep and verify it uses collected assets rather than the old disk locations.
Audit installed fonts, effects, scripts, external 3D textures, render destinations, proxies and dynamically linked dependencies. Collect Files is not a guarantee of third-party plugin portability.
Generate an explicit README listing AE version 25.6, frame rates, render settings, color management, input dependencies, licensed assets and any known limitations.
Use versioned project saves such as Project_v001.aep and Increment and Save; maintain automated backups where configured. Restore a backup before trusting the process.
Consider making a high-quality pre-render or flattened proof video for reviewers who cannot open AE. Keep editable project and rendered approval media separate.
checks: I can collect and reopen a project from a new path.
I have a dependency manifest.
I can restore a previous project version.
chapters.experiment: Move the collected package to a different drive/path and re-open all comps without missing-file dialogs.
pitfalls: Collect Files does not bundle Adobe subscription licenses or every installed plugin.
An .aep file by itself often cannot reproduce a project.

chapters.title: 33 · Performance, memory, cache and proxies
chapters.why: Optimize the actual bottleneck instead of deleting caches reflexively.
steps: Save a slow experiment project. Time a cold preview and a repeated warm preview over the same work area before changing settings.
Set viewer resolution Half or Quarter for fast interaction when appropriate; note that changing view quality does not automatically guarantee a full-resolution final render.

Inspect Edit → Preferences → Memory & Performance and Disk Cache settings. Reserve adequate RAM for Windows, choose a fast drive with spare capacity, and understand that purging invalidates useful cached frames.
Compare one CPU-bound procedural effect, GPU-accelerated effect, and codec-decoding bottleneck. Watch whether performance changes when an effect switch is turned off.
Use proxy footage or pre-renders for expensive sources and comps when appropriate. Keep a clear replacement/restore path so that final output uses the intended sources.

Check Multi-Frame Rendering and limitations of plugins. For a pathological project, disable suspect third-party effects one at a time and test safe startup rather than assuming the GPU always causes slowdowns.
checks: I can separate first render from cached preview.
I can find RAM and disk-cache settings.
I can make a measurable performance comparison.
chapters.experiment: Create a before/after timing sheet for a 5-second heavy effects comp with two controlled optimization changes.
pitfalls: Clearing the disk cache can make a project slower temporarily.
A faster SSD does not cure an expensive single-frame effect algorithm.

chapters.title: 34 · Diagnose broken results systematically
chapters.why: Identify whether a problem is source, interpretation, transform, matte, effect, render or environment.
steps: When the Comp viewer is black, check active comp, time, layer In/Out, eye, solo, opacity, mask, matte, blend mode and viewer channel before touching effects.
If the result is different after precomposing, compare render order, collapse transformations, effect stacks, adjustment layer scope and color management.
If preview is frozen, disable Caps Lock, inspect Preview settings and work area, then confirm a frame has been rendered. Restart only after a simple reproducible check.
If an effect is missing, inspect Effect Manager, plugin installation, 8/16/32-bpc support and whether it was introduced after 25.6. Replace unsupported features rather than inventing a hidden menu.
If output differs from Comp viewer, compare Render Settings, Output Module, output color space, channel selection, renderer and file playback transform.
Create a reduced reproducible .aep by duplicating the comp and removing half of its layers/effects, repeatedly narrowing the issue. Save before deleting or purging.
checks: I can isolate a black-frame cause.
I can compare viewer/render settings.
I can build a minimal reproduction.
chapters.experiment: Intentionally hide a layer with a matte and an effect, then diagnose the failure in a fixed checklist without random clicking.
pitfalls: A render queue completion message means the job finished, not that visual, alpha or audio QC passed.
Caps Lock can inhibit viewer updates.

chapters.title: 35 · Complete project: 10-second motion graphics composite
chapters.why: Combine foundations, animation, keying, data, effects, sound and export into a repeatable deliverable.
steps: Create a clearly labeled 1920×1080 24 fps comp called FINAL_10S. Import or generate a 10-second background, a branded shape/title, and short WAV music/sound effects; keep the source files in project Assets.
Build a 2-second introductory title. Use a masked or matted reveal, controlled easing, and motion blur. Keep typography clear and safe from frame edges.
At 2–6 seconds, animate a set of three cards with a Null controller and either a text animator or template-driven properties. Make their timing editable without rebuilding the graphic.

Add a short compositing moment: tracked corner-pin insert, a keyed subject or a clean roto. Do not fake one if source footage is unavailable; use a self-generated shape/matte demonstration and document the substitution.
At 6–9 seconds, finish a procedural transition using Fractal Noise, Displacement Map or Glow. Audio should enter and leave cleanly, and the last second should contain a readable final message.

Audit at Full resolution: typography, alpha edges, layer order, no one-frame flash, camera position, color and clipping. Render a review movie and an archival-quality master; collect project files and write a delivery note.
checks: I can deliver a complete timeline.
My project reopens without missing assets.
I can explain every element and effect in the render.
chapters.experiment: Grade yourself: can you rebuild 80% of the sequence from scratch with your own footage and no tutorial?
pitfalls: Do not judge a project only by rendered appearance; reproducibility and clean dependencies matter.
Use the exact 25.6 feature set throughout.

topics.title: Version discipline: AE 25.6, not 26.x
topics.summary: A reproducible workflow must target only controls available in the November 2025 release.

sections.title: Verify the build
sections.text: After Effects 25.6 shipped in November 2025. Use Help → About After Effects to inspect the installed version. A menu described in 2026 Adobe Help may not exist in 25.6, even if a modern user guide says it is standard.

sections.title: Available by 25.6
sections.text: 25.2 brought improved high-performance playback, HDR preview and FBX import; 25.3 smoother viewer zoom; 25.4 Quick Offset, text formatting copy/paste and CICP metadata; 25.5 mostly fixes; 25.6 the shared 3D gizmo, default camera settings, Tip of the Day and timeline housekeeping.

sections.title: Not available
sections.text: 26.0+ introduces native parametric meshes, new audio Compressor/Gate/Distortion, native SVG shapes, variable-font axes, and Unmult; 26.2 adds Object Matte, Quick Apply and proportional scrubbing; 26.3 adds Curl Noise, improved Mask Tracker, Advanced 3D engine DOF and clipboard-frame capture; 26.5 adds new guides, modern effect labels and ACES 2.0 bundling.

topics.experiment: Search Adobe feature history for a favorite feature and record the version where it first appeared.
pitfalls: An old After Effects 25.x project may still load in 26.x; that does not mean 26.x features back-port to 25.6.

topics.title: What is distinctive about 25.6
topics.summary: Four practical improvements and a major compatibility note.

sections.title: Shared 3D gizmo
sections.text: Select multiple 3D layers and use a single viewport gizmo to position, rotate and scale multiple selected layers. It reduces visual clutter; it does not replace Parenting or create a persistent Group object.

sections.title: Default camera settings
sections.text: View menu allows modifying default-camera behavior for appropriate views. Use this to control perspective when no explicit camera is used or when viewing a custom view, but record the change in a training project.

sections.title: Interface and fixes
sections.text: Tip of the Day appears when an appropriate viewer is empty/reloaded. Timelines can be closed to the left or right, and 25.6 fixes a large group of project, export and stability defects.

sections.title: GPU boundary
sections.text: Adobe’s 25.x requirements specify that After Effects 25.6 requires OpenCL 2.0 where OpenCL is applicable, removing support for 1.2 or older. Hardware compatibility matters more than incidental new tool names.

topics.experiment: Make a two-layer 3D scene and operate the joint gizmo, then parent both layers to a Null and describe the difference.

topics.title: The Windows After Effects interface
topics.summary: Know the difference between each panel and where focus lives.

sections.title: Project and composition
sections.text: The Project panel stores footage, comps and folders. Composition viewer shows a rendered view of one composition at a given time, with guides and on-canvas controls. Double-clicking footage opens the Footage panel; double-clicking a footage layer can open the Layer panel.

sections.title: Timeline and Effects
sections.text: Timeline hosts layers, track mattes, time spans, properties, expressions, keyframes and graph curves. Effect Controls displays the selected layer’s effect stack; Effects & Presets is a catalog/search area for available effects and animation presets.

sections.title: Focused shortcuts
sections.text: A key can mean something else in text editing, painting, a 3D view or a render queue. Ctrl+D duplicates the current selected object in the active context. Click the intended panel and verify selection before using a destructive command.

sections.title: Recover layouts
sections.text: Use the Window → Workspace menu, reset layouts, hover a panel and press backtick to maximize it. F4 reveals alternate Timeline Switches/Modes columns. Use panel tabs and viewer locks to compare related comps.

topics.experiment: Use only keyboard and workspace menus to locate Project, Preview, Character, Render Queue and Composition panels in 60 seconds.
pitfalls: A gray blank panel may be a viewer without an open item, not a failed render.

topics.title: Composition, layer and project hierarchy
topics.summary: Understand nested composition references and editable source instances.

sections.title: Files are not embedded automatically
sections.text: An .aep project points to sources and stores transformations and project data. Two layers can reference one source item, and two comps can nest the same precomp; changing the nested original impacts both copies unless overridden.

sections.title: What lives on a layer
sections.text: A layer has In/Out, transform, masks, effects, blending mode, mattes, switches, parenting, keyframes and other type-specific properties. Effects modify generated pixel data; they are not identical to a shape layer’s Contents operators.

sections.title: Comp settings affect interpretation
sections.text: Composition FPS defines its frame grid; resolution and pixel aspect determine the render canvas. The footage source has its own interpretation, while the comp layer instance has its own transform and time placement.

topics.experiment: Build two comps sharing a precomp, then alter the shared precomp artwork and observe both.
pitfalls: Do not assume deleting a layer will delete its Project footage source.

topics.title: Folders, naming and backup policy
topics.summary: Organize projects so someone else can rebuild them.

sections.title: On disk vs Project panel
sections.text: A Project folder is metadata inside .aep, not necessarily an OS directory. Keep named Windows folders for Assets, Renders, Cache if desired, Archive and Collected. Backups should be saved outside the active working folder where feasible.

sections.title: Naming schemes
sections.text: Give comps distinctive prefixes (FINAL_, SCENE_, PRE_, CTRL_) and avoid duplicate or confusing names for controllers used in expressions. Label colors aid navigation but must not be the only source of meaning.

sections.title: Reproducibility
sections.text: Use File → Dependencies → Collect Files for used source material; also list external fonts, plugins, LUTs, environment assets and scripts. Never claim Collect Files packages plugin binaries or licenses.

topics.experiment: Open an .aep from a moved Collect Files directory after severing access to its original Assets path.
pitfalls: Save As is not identical to Increment and Save or Collect Files.

topics.title: Import formats, sequences and linked files
topics.summary: Always inspect time, channels, format and external dependencies.

sections.title: Footage vs layer
sections.text: Importing creates a footage item in Project. Dragging it into a composition creates a layer instance with its own in point, transform and effects. Deleting an instance does not necessarily delete the source item.

sections.title: Sequence and alpha
sections.text: Numbered images can become one time-based sequence. Check whether alpha is straight or premultiplied; a premultiplied RGB fringe should not be interpreted as an image with independent straight edge colors.

sections.title: Dynamic links and layered PSD/AI
sections.text: Where supported, import a layered image as Composition — Retain Layer Sizes to keep logical layers. Inspect the anchor and coordinate placement after the import. Dynamic Link/Photoshop/Illustrator updates need the original source app/assets.

topics.experiment: Import a five-frame PNG sequence and then import one frame as still; explain the difference.
pitfalls: A media path under Downloads can disappear even if .aep continues to exist.

topics.title: Footage frame rate, alpha and pixel aspect
topics.summary: Bad interpretation can invalidate an otherwise perfect composite.

sections.title: Frame rates
sections.text: When footage is interpreted at a different FPS, it may run faster/slower. Time stretch and frame blending are different from reinterpretation. Variable-frame-rate recordings may need transcoding to constant frame rate.

sections.title: Alpha types
sections.text: Straight/unmatted pixels encode RGB independently of alpha. Premultiplied/matted pixels were already mixed against a matte color; interpreting them incorrectly often creates dark/light halos.

sections.title: Pixel aspect and fields
sections.text: A non-square pixel interpretation scales geometry, not just final output dimensions. Interlaced fields and separated-fields options matter for legacy broadcast material and can cause combing if interpreted wrong.

topics.experiment: Take an RGBA still, intentionally choose incorrect alpha interpretation, then restore a clean edge.
pitfalls: Changing footage interpretation can affect every use of that footage item.

topics.title: FPS, timecode and frame alignment
topics.summary: Work in frame counts to avoid off-by-one visual errors.

sections.title: Timecode
sections.text: In a 24-fps non-drop-frame composition, 00:00:01:12 means 1.5 seconds. Frames within a second run 00 through 23. The display mode can also show frames rather than timecode.

sections.title: Layer sampling
sections.text: Source footage at 30 fps inside a 24-fps comp is sampled at the comp frame grid, potentially repeating/dropping frames or using blending. Audio is time-based and should be inspected independently of visual frame matching.

sections.title: Useful arithmetic
sections.text: Duration seconds = frames / fps. 72 frames at 24 fps = 3 seconds; 100 frames at 25 fps = 4 seconds. Use the guide’s frame calculator to explore rates and offsets.

topics.experiment: Make a four-second comp at 25 fps and label frame numbers 0, 24, 25, 99, 100 with timeline markers.
pitfalls: Drop-frame timecode applies to appropriate broadcast rates; do not use its punctuation as a universal frame-count formula.

topics.title: Layer bounds, work areas and markers
topics.summary: A timeline is several overlapping time systems.

sections.title: Three positions
sections.text: The composition playhead indicates comp time; the layer’s bar shows In/Out times in that comp; footage source time indicates which source frame is used. A precomp also has its own inner timeline.

sections.title: Move versus trim
sections.text: [ and ] reposition entire selected layers to CTI using their In/Out references; Alt+[ and Alt+] trim at CTI. Ctrl+Shift+D splits. These are not equivalent to moving animation keyframes only.

sections.title: Markers and work area
sections.text: B/N set work area ends for local preview/render planning. Main keyboard digits may navigate numbered comp markers, while numpad keys can select layers or start a preview depending on focus.

topics.experiment: Use one video clip to demonstrate a shift, a trim, a split and a work-area change, and label each in a separate comp.
pitfalls: Changing the work area does not necessarily change comp duration.

topics.title: Coordinates, anchor points and transforms
topics.summary: Be precise about which point and which coordinate system each value uses.

sections.title: Anchor versus position
sections.text: Anchor is in the layer’s own coordinate system; Position specifies the anchor in parent/comp coordinates. Moving an anchor can appear to shift the image unless AE compensates its Position when using Pan Behind.

sections.title: Transform nesting
sections.text: A shape group has its own Transform inside Contents, plus the layer Transform. A child layer uses parent-space Position; a 3D layer can have X/Y/Z and Orientation as well as Rotation values.

sections.title: Converting positions
sections.text: Expressions provide toComp(), fromComp(), toWorld(), fromWorld() and related methods for correct cross-coordinate conversion. A direct Position link is only straightforward when both properties share the same coordinate context.

topics.experiment: Find the same corner of a shape before/after parenting and explain why its displayed Position values differ.
pitfalls: A shape rectangle size is not the same property as layer Scale.

topics.title: Parenting, nulls and reusable rigs
topics.summary: Use simple controllers to coordinate several layers safely.

sections.title: Parent-child relationships
sections.text: A child inherits transforms from its parent but retains independent local animation. Parent to a Null for a clean control layer rather than applying identical Position keyframes to every object.

sections.title: Controllers
sections.text: Use descriptive names and Expression Controls for user-facing parameters. Parent a child only once in a hierarchy; avoid creating circular dependencies through expressions.

sections.title: Rig safety
sections.text: Duplicate a rig and check whether expressions reference the duplicated or original controls. Essential Properties are often more suitable for controlled per-instance variation than unstructured cross-comp expressions.

topics.experiment: Build a three-layer clock where the root null travels while a hand rotates independently.
pitfalls: Parenting a 3D child to a 2D null can have unexpected coordinate behavior; test and document.

topics.title: Keyframes and interpolation
topics.summary: A keyframe stores a property value at a specific time.

sections.title: Recording properties
sections.text: Enable the stopwatch when you mean to animate. At a new time, editing the value creates an additional key. Changing a static value before enabling a stopwatch does not record a time history.

sections.title: Interpolation
sections.text: Linear changes at uniform numeric rate, Hold jumps, Bézier allows easing. Rotation angle and 2D Position follow different units, so similar graphs can still produce different perceived motion.

sections.title: Keyframe housekeeping
sections.text: U reveals keyed properties, J/K navigate visible time events, and Ctrl+Shift+K opens velocity controls. Ctrl-click in a keyframe view is contextual; learn the specific mode before editing.

topics.experiment: Make the same 0-to-100 opacity transition with Linear, Hold and Easy Ease.
pitfalls: Clicking the active stopwatch deletes all animation for that property.

topics.title: Value Graph, Speed Graph and easing
topics.summary: Control velocity and rhythm separately from endpoint positions.

sections.title: Speed vs value
sections.text: A Value Graph plots the property value over time. A Speed Graph plots the rate of change. A flat speed graph can correspond to a sloped linear position value graph.

sections.title: Influence and handles
sections.text: Temporal Bézier handles control easing at keys. At a given duration, sharper influence usually shifts which portions of the journey happen quickly versus slowly. The path can remain straight.

sections.title: Spatial keys
sections.text: Position motion paths have separate spatial Bézier interpolation; a curved trajectory does not guarantee ease. Rove Across Time can redistribute intermediate spatial keys but not arbitrary hold or non-spatial properties.

topics.experiment: Animate three identical dots to the same endpoint with different arrival timing and explain the change in speed graph.
pitfalls: Do not make a curved spatial path when you only need easing.

topics.title: Timing and design principles for readable motion
topics.summary: Make movement communicate hierarchy, not merely demonstrate tools.

sections.title: Pose and hold
sections.text: Allow time for reading after a title enters. Motion that never stops is often harder to follow; a clean hold creates hierarchy and reduces attention fatigue.

sections.title: Overlap and anticipation
sections.text: Offset related layer animation by a few frames using measured timing, not arbitrary random delays. For a 24-fps comp, 6 frames = 0.25 seconds; choose offsets based on readability.

sections.title: Consistent motion language
sections.text: Keep easing, direction, acceleration and stagger rules reusable across a project. Test at full playback speed and also frame by frame for collisions.

topics.experiment: Build a 3-card entrance with 5-frame staggers and consistent ease-out shapes.
pitfalls: Excess overshoot can look like accidental jitter rather than controlled energy.

topics.title: Parametric shapes vs Bézier paths
topics.summary: Use the least complicated editable geometry for each job.

sections.title: Shape structure
sections.text: Shape Layer → Contents contains groups. Each group may contain path, fill, stroke, group transform and operators; the layer has its own Transform independently.

sections.title: Keep parameters live
sections.text: Rectangle Path Size and Roundness allow reusable UI-like cards. Polystar Path lets you animate point count and radii. Converting to Bézier gives vertex freedom but sacrifices simple parametric controls.

sections.title: Operators
sections.text: Trim Paths draws strokes; Repeater duplicates source shapes; Offset Paths grows/shrinks outlines; Pucker & Bloat distorts forms. They operate in Contents, not standard effects stack.

topics.experiment: Construct a shape-based progress ring, then change its size without redrawing vertices.
pitfalls: A filled closed path revealed with Trim Paths may not behave like a stroked outline.

topics.title: Masks, shape paths and motion paths
topics.summary: Three different kinds of path can look visually similar.

sections.title: Mask path
sections.text: A mask path defines visible pixels and has Mode, Feather, Opacity and Expansion. Mask Path keyframes animate that outline, not the layer Position itself.

sections.title: Shape path
sections.text: A Shape Path defines fill/stroke geometry and can be a live parametric outline or a vertex-editable Bézier curve. It can be copied between compatible path properties in many situations.

sections.title: Motion path
sections.text: A Position property with spatial animation creates a trajectory whose dots represent temporal samples. Its vertices and handles change spatial travel, while keyframes/Graph Editor define timing.

topics.experiment: Make one letter follow a mask path while a separate shape traces a closed path via Trim Paths.
pitfalls: Do not assume two visually similar paths have interchangeable parameter types.

topics.title: Shape strokes, Trim Paths and Write-on
topics.summary: Choose between drawing geometry and painting pixels.

sections.title: Stroke types
sections.text: Shape Stroke is vector line styling inside a Shape Layer. The Stroke effect can reveal a mask path on footage or a solid. Write-on uses paint-like accumulation and has its own timing controls.

sections.title: Dashed paths
sections.text: A shape stroke can have dashes, caps, joins and taper depending on the shape controls. Trim Paths Start/End define the visible portion of a path, while Offset rotates this visible window.

sections.title: Compositing
sections.text: To make a tracked outline, first track/animate the path, then generate a stroke, then optionally add Glow. Use a solid or precomp so the stroke has enough output dimensions when necessary.
