topics.experiment: Draw a six-stroke icon and animate strokes in a deliberate order.
pitfalls: Do not use a high-feather mask in place of a designed stroke.

topics.title: Mask modes and feathering
topics.summary: Masks edit layer transparency while preserving source pixels.

sections.title: Mode logic
sections.text: Add reveals, Subtract removes, Intersect retains shared area. Inverted changes interpretation. With multiple masks, compositing behavior depends on mode, ordering and the layer’s alpha.

sections.title: Edge controls
sections.text: Feather produces a soft transition, Expansion dilates/erodes region borders and Mask Opacity scales contribution. Variable/per-vertex feathering can handle nonuniform boundaries.

sections.title: Animated masks
sections.text: With a selected mask path stopwatch, edit vertices over time. Fewer stable vertices generally track better than dozens of imprecise ones.

topics.experiment: Draw two masks: one additive and one subtractive, then isolate the overlap.
pitfalls: If masks are invisible, check View → Show Layer Controls; it does not change pixels.

topics.title: Alpha, straight RGB and premultiplication
topics.summary: Transparency is separate from visible RGB even when pixels look black.

sections.title: Representation
sections.text: An RGBA pixel stores red, green, blue and alpha. Alpha=0 need not force RGB=0 in all representations. In straight alpha, RGB is often intended unmultiplied; premultiplied RGB already contains transparency/color matte interaction.

sections.title: Artifacts
sections.text: Dark outlines on translucent edges commonly result from misinterpreted alpha or resampling a matte-color-contaminated source. Inspect straight RGB and alpha separately before adding choker/blur.

sections.title: Delivery
sections.text: A codec/container must carry an alpha plane, and the output module must export RGB+Alpha correctly. Many MP4 H.264 workflows do not carry ordinary RGBA transparency.

topics.experiment: Create a white semi-transparent circle over black, export and test its edge over magenta.
pitfalls: Using Screen blending for black-backed particles is not identical to producing alpha for downstream editors.

topics.title: Alpha/luma track mattes
topics.summary: An independent matte layer controls another layer’s visibility.

sections.title: Alpha matte
sections.text: Visible matte alpha determines the target’s coverage. A red opaque matte and blue opaque matte cover equally if both have full alpha.

sections.title: Luma matte
sections.text: Luminance of a matte determines visibility. Black gives none and white gives full coverage; mid-gray gives partial coverage. Color gradients can behave unlike alpha-only gradients.

sections.title: Flexible setup
sections.text: Modern track mattes let the target reference an appropriate other layer in the comp. One matte may be reused in more than one place; keep the source named and be aware of comp boundaries.

topics.experiment: Use a checkerboard, a full-alpha red rectangle and a grayscale gradient to compare alpha and luma mattes.
pitfalls: A mask on the footage and a matte sourced from a different layer are not identical workflows.

topics.title: Layer blend modes and compositing
topics.summary: Blend math changes RGB interaction with layers beneath.

sections.title: Ordinary compositing
sections.text: Normal combines pixels by alpha. Multiply darkens based on RGB product; Screen generally lightens; Add sums channels and can clip or exceed normal ranges in high-bit-depth projects.

sections.title: Order matters
sections.text: A blend mode acts on a layer relative to what has been composited below it. Reordering layers often changes the look, even when no keyframes change.

sections.title: Alpha does not follow automatically
sections.text: Screening a black-background explosion may visually hide black but does not magically reconstruct fully useful alpha. Check the deliverable’s requirements.

topics.experiment: Composite a bright flare onto black footage with Screen, then try a true RGBA flare and compare downstream alpha.
pitfalls: Blend modes can behave differently under linear-light color management.

topics.title: Effect and transform evaluation order
topics.summary: The order of pixel processing explains why precomps can change results.

sections.title: Processing chain
sections.text: A simplified layer flow considers source, masks and effects, transformations, layer styles and compositing. Actual order can vary with layer type, 3D renderer and continuously rasterized/precomp settings.

sections.title: Precompose effects
sections.text: Moving effects inside versus leaving them outside a precomp can shift which pixels are processed at what scale/geometry. Use two simple controls to prove the cause.

sections.title: Adjustments and nested comps
sections.text: An adjustment layer affects pixels composited beneath it inside its active group/context. Nesting can change what image it receives and where it is calculated.

topics.experiment: Apply a 20-pixel blur to a 100×100 square, scale 500%, then swap where blur and scale occur.
pitfalls: Collapse Transformations can change rendering; it should not be turned on reflexively.

topics.title: Precomposition and nested timeline logic
topics.summary: A precomp is a composition used as a layer in another comp.

sections.title: Two contexts
sections.text: Inner composition time, resolution, frame rate, layer transforms and effects can all differ from the outer master comp. Time Remapping on outer precomp changes sampled inner time.

sections.title: Move attributes choice
sections.text: When precomposing, whether attributes move into the new comp changes how/where an effect is evaluated. Test with one blur and one transform rather than memorizing the dialog without context.

sections.title: Maintainable nesting
sections.text: Keep comp hierarchies shallow enough to inspect. Prefix names, write purposeful notes and avoid accidentally creating expression dependencies across unstable names.

topics.experiment: Build a comp of an animated icon, use it twice, and override only one instance’s timing.
pitfalls: Do not assume outer frames and inner frames line up without checking frame-rate and start-time behavior.

topics.title: The effect stack and control surfaces
topics.summary: Each effect consumes the prior rendered result in its layer context.

sections.title: Processing order
sections.text: Fractal Noise → Levels → Glow does not necessarily match Fractal Noise → Glow → Levels. The first can threshold which regions glow; the second can recolor/clamp the already glowing output.

sections.title: Effect Controls
sections.text: Use F3 to inspect, rename and reorder effect instances. The fx switch bypasses individual effects and the layer fx switch bypasses effects as a set; deleting all effects is destructive.

sections.title: Scope
sections.text: A blur on a source layer differs from a blur on a precomp or an adjustment layer. Effect operating bounds, alpha and precomp render order can change the visible result.

topics.experiment: Reverse two effects on a duplicate layer and explain the changed pixels.
pitfalls: Do not treat a property expression as an image effect.

topics.title: Effects, presets and compatibility
topics.summary: Read the difference between native effects, bundled plugins and third-party plugins.

sections.title: Find capabilities
sections.text: Effects & Presets lists installed effects and presets. Different AE releases can add/remove or deprecate items. The Adobe Effect List reports GPU, Multi-Frame Rendering and bpc support for many named effects, but is a rolling document.

sections.title: Predesigned animation
sections.text: Presets may create multiple effects, text animators or keyframes. Apply them to a disposable layer and inspect what changed before using them on a production layer.

sections.title: Manage failures
sections.text: If an effect is missing, investigate Effect Manager, plugin licensing, paths, bit depth and OS support. A disabled or obsolete effect can still appear on old layers.

topics.experiment: Apply one animation preset to a temporary text layer, inspect every parameter it added, then rebuild its visual behavior manually.
pitfalls: An effect may render on CPU even in a GPU-capable composition.

topics.title: Adjustment layers and global looks
topics.summary: Place finishing looks intentionally in a layer stack.

sections.title: What they sample
sections.text: Adjustment layers take the composite below within their scope and process it through effects. Use them to keep repeated color/grain/blur calculations under control.

sections.title: Limiting scope
sections.text: Trim adjustment In/Out, use masks or mattes, or nest intended layers into a precomp so only that result receives the change.

sections.title: Adjustment vs solid
sections.text: A solid with an effect is still an ordinary image source unless effect/composite settings cause it to act differently. An adjustment layer is a special processing layer.

topics.experiment: Apply Curves to only one card via an adjustment layer mask and compare to a directly applied effect.
pitfalls: If the adjustment layer is at the bottom of the comp, it cannot affect layers above it as expected.

topics.title: Gaussian, lens and map-driven blur
topics.summary: Pick a blur that expresses the actual desired motion/depth.

sections.title: Ordinary blur
sections.text: Gaussian Blur is predictable and often economical. Directional Blur resembles linear streaking; Radial Blur simulates radial spin/zoom; Unsharp Mask enhances edges rather than smoothing.

sections.title: Lens look
sections.text: Camera Lens Blur can shape bokeh highlights and blur-map-dependent focus. It may be more expensive than a Gaussian blur; test representative shots and settings.

sections.title: Blur a matte vs blur an image
sections.text: Softening a mask/matte edge preserves subject detail differently from blurring the subject RGB itself. Use the channel viewer to see what data changed.

topics.experiment: Create an alpha matte with a 20-pixel soft edge, compare against a 20-pixel Gaussian blur on the actual footage.
pitfalls: Overblurred matte edges can produce transparent halos with colored source pixels.

topics.title: Fractal/Turbulent Noise and displacement
topics.summary: Generate repeatable organic texture and use it as a controlled signal.

sections.title: Noise generator
sections.text: Fractal Noise exposes a procedural field. Contrast, Brightness, Scale, Complexity and Evolution/Offset Turbulence change pattern appearance and motion.

sections.title: Signal map
sections.text: Convert noise to useful grayscale and plug into Displacement Map, Compound Blur or matte controls. The map does not need to look beautiful as a layer; its luminance/channel relationship is the important factor.

sections.title: Animation loops
sections.text: Looping Evolution might not produce a seamless visual loop unless cycling and offset settings are chosen correctly. Check first and last frame against each other.

topics.experiment: Make 3 kinds of noise with identical Evolution speed but different Scale and use each as a Displacement Map.
pitfalls: Curl Noise first appears in 26.3; it is not a 25.6 effect.

topics.title: Displacement, depth and faux 3D
topics.summary: Depth maps encode local differences but do not automatically turn an image into geometry.

sections.title: Grayscale meaning
sections.text: A depth map typically uses light/dark values to represent a chosen near/far ordering. It is only meaningful when an effect interprets those values with a known range and channel.

sections.title: 2D parallax
sections.text: Use separately cut foreground/background layers, Z positions and a moving camera for actual AE 2.5D parallax. A displacement map instead repositions pixels inside a layer.

sections.title: Map quality
sections.text: Soft gradients can create smooth wipes or depth-based blur. Abrupt low-resolution boundaries cause distortion and halos; feather the map before it is sampled.

topics.experiment: Create a grayscale radial gradient and use it as a blur map, then as a displacement map; compare interpretations.
pitfalls: Camera Lens Blur on a map is not Advanced 3D camera depth of field.

topics.title: Time remapping, reversal and loops
topics.summary: Resampling a source in time is different from moving keys along a comp timeline.

sections.title: Source-clock changes
sections.text: Time Remap keys map comp time to source time. A hold segment samples one source frame repeatedly; a descending segment can reverse the footage.

sections.title: Layer vs keyframe reversal
sections.text: Time-Reverse Layer reverses the layer source playback; Time-Reverse Keyframes reverses timing of selected animation keys. Use deliberately named test duplicates.

sections.title: Loop frames
sections.text: The source-duration end time can be one frame after the last visible frame. Fix end keys before applying loopOut('cycle') on a Time Remap property to avoid seam flashes.

topics.experiment: Render a 2-second clip as forward, reverse, freeze and looping examples.
pitfalls: Video source frames may be interpolated differently depending on frame blending settings.

topics.title: Native motion blur and shutter settings
topics.summary: Motion blur communicates movement between discrete frames.

sections.title: Two switches
sections.text: Layer Motion Blur switch must be enabled, and the comp master Motion Blur must also be on. Some source/effect types require separate blur solutions.

sections.title: Shutter angle
sections.text: Larger shutter angle generally creates longer smears relative to frame interval. Shutter phase changes the sampling timing relative to the frame center.

sections.title: Evaluate carefully
sections.text: Check blur at final frame rate and Full-quality rendering, not only in a low-resolution interactive preview. Camera/3D motion may need renderer-compatible blur.

topics.experiment: Render the same fast-moving square with motion blur off, modest shutter, and long shutter.
pitfalls: Motion blur cannot repair extremely poor source motion tracking.

topics.title: Point/box text, metrics and typography
topics.summary: Readable type depends on spacing and consistent layout.

sections.title: Text modes
sections.text: Point text grows as you type; paragraph text wraps inside a bounding box. Baseline shift, leading, kerning, tracking and paragraph alignment are distinct tools.

sections.title: Design rules
sections.text: Build with type hierarchy, padding and safe areas. Validate font availability, substitution behavior and variable dimensions of different language strings.

sections.title: Editable workflows
sections.text: Preserve editable text for templates and handoff. Only convert text to shapes when vertex-specific path animation or flattening is truly required; a shape conversion is no longer a normal editable text string.

topics.experiment: Fit three differently sized names into one title-card layout without manual per-name repositioning.
pitfalls: Style controls and font metrics can change between installed font versions.

topics.title: Text animators and selectors
topics.summary: Text animation has selectors inside the text layer hierarchy.

sections.title: Animator vs source
sections.text: Source Text defines content. Text → Animate adds a group of animated properties that apply to selected characters, words or lines. The layer Transform moves all characters together.

sections.title: Range selector
sections.text: Start, End, Offset and Advanced selectors determine which text is affected. Shape, Smoothness and Based On modes can create scans, typewriter-like reveals or per-word emphasis.

sections.title: Expression selector
sections.text: A custom selector can provide per-character weight values. Use it only when Range or Wiggly Selector cannot express the motion and maintain it carefully.

topics.experiment: Animate each word in a heading by changing only Based On and a range selector’s Offset.
pitfalls: Variable-font axis animation is a 26.0 addition, not a 25.6 skill.

topics.title: Kinetic typography and text clarity
topics.summary: Text animation is meaningful only when it stays legible.

sections.title: Sequence hierarchy
sections.text: Decide which line is primary and which is secondary. Do not animate every word with equal force; use emphasis selectively.

sections.title: Spacing and contrast
sections.text: Monitor text at target playback size, on a phone-sized viewer when applicable. Check antialiasing, safe zones and contrast on busy plates.

sections.title: Time constraints
sections.text: Estimate reading time and keep titles visible long enough to understand. Faster keyframes do not automatically make a better design.

topics.experiment: Make an 8-second quote with 2-second line holds, one emphasized word per line, and a consistent baseline.
pitfalls: Scale bounces can produce text shimmer at small final sizes.

topics.title: Audio preview, sync and output
topics.summary: Work with sound deliberately even when AE is not the main editing app.

sections.title: Layers and waveforms
sections.text: L reveals levels; LL reveals waveform. Preview shortcuts differ by normal keyboard and numeric keypad. Set markers to real audible onsets instead of guessing from peaks.

sections.title: Sync
sections.text: Layer shifting, Time Stretch and frame-rate interpretation can all affect where sound aligns with motion. Video footage with variable frame rate can create sync trouble and may need preprocessing.

sections.title: Final QC
sections.text: Enable audio in the export path and listen to the rendered file. Verify beginning/end fades, clipping and the intended channel mix, not just a loud waveform in Timeline.

topics.experiment: Synchronize three shape pops to audible beats and export with checked audio sync.
pitfalls: After Effects audio tools do not replace a full multitrack audio editing/mixing environment.

topics.title: Convert Audio to Keyframes workflow
topics.summary: Use an audio amplitude slider to drive numeric properties.

sections.title: Generate amplitude
sections.text: Use Animation → Keyframe Assistant → Convert Audio to Keyframes. The generated Null holds Left, Right and Both Channels Slider keyframes.

sections.title: Map scale
sections.text: On Scale, reference Both Channels with an expression and map/clamp it into an appropriate scale range. Use `[s,s]` for 2D scale output, not a bare number.

sections.title: Noise control
sections.text: Raw amplitude changes rapidly; smooth it or drive sparse pulses to avoid uncomfortable shaking. Add an envelope/falloff rather than directly following every sample.

topics.experiment: Make a circle pulse between 100% and 135% based on a short drum loop.
pitfalls: Volume level curves do not identify rhythm genre or musical beat positions automatically.

topics.title: Keylight, spill and edge recovery
topics.summary: Clean keying has separate stages with distinct failure modes.

sections.title: Source stage
sections.text: Even lighting and sufficient chroma separation reduce the work of keying. Add a garbage matte so the keyer only processes the relevant area.

sections.title: Alpha stage
sections.text: Keylight Screen Matte lets you inspect and refine the core silhouette. Avoid clipping all hair detail for a perfectly black background.

sections.title: Edge stage
sections.text: Key Cleaner, Advanced Spill Suppressor, subtle edge color correction and selective blur improve integration. Test against multiple backgrounds and moving frames.

topics.experiment: Key a person over a dark and a light background, then adjust edges until both look acceptable.
pitfalls: Green spill suppression is a color correction problem, not only alpha thresholding.

topics.title: Roto Brush and Refine Edge in 25.6
topics.summary: Use the available AI-assisted roto workflow without 26.2 Object Matte.

sections.title: Layer viewer
sections.text: Roto Brush strokes are made on a layer in the Layer panel, not drawn as a Composition viewer shape. The initial base frame guides propagation across nearby frames.

sections.title: Propagation and correction
sections.text: Inspect forward/backward spans, repair slips and use Refine Edge for wispy hair. Freeze after corrections and render check the entire selection range.

sections.title: Tool choice
sections.text: For a rigid object, a tracked mask or Mocha planar mask may be more efficient than broad Roto Brush propagation. Choose based on edge topology and motion.

topics.experiment: Roto a walking person for two seconds without any abrupt matte popping.
pitfalls: Object Matte AI selection did not ship until 26.2.

topics.title: Point tracking, attach points and drift
topics.summary: Understand what one or two tracked features can and cannot tell you.

sections.title: Feature region
sections.text: Contains visual detail the tracker matches across frames. Search region defines where it is allowed to search. Attach Point is the actual point used to transfer the solved motion.

sections.title: Motion types
sections.text: One point provides translation, two points can model more of rotation and scale. Perspective corner changes require an appropriate perspective/planar tracking workflow.

sections.title: Review
sections.text: Watch each tracked frame for drift. Reducing motion blur, tracking in segments or choosing a more stable high-contrast target can improve results.

topics.experiment: Attach a 30×30 crosshair to a moving shirt button and keep it aligned for 60 frames.
pitfalls: A search region that is too small will lose a fast-moving feature.

topics.title: Mocha AE planar tracking
topics.summary: Planar trackers follow a textured surface rather than one point.

sections.title: Planar region
sections.text: Define a useful plane, follow stable texture and manage occlusion. Mocha surface corners are not the same thing as the drawn tracking spline.

sections.title: Export/copy
sections.text: Use the bundled Mocha AE integration’s supported transfer path to Corner Pin or transform data. Check exact plugin UI for the installed Mocha build.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: A bent cloth or independently moving object is not one stable plane. Break up the track or choose Roto Brush/manual work rather than forcing a single planar solve.

topics.experiment: Track a poster on a wall and apply a four-corner grid in AE.
pitfalls: Warp Stabilizer, 3D Camera Tracker and Mocha each solve different geometric problems.

topics.title: Warp Stabilizer and camera motion
topics.summary: Smooth shaky footage without destroying the composition.

sections.title: What it analyzes
sections.text: Warp Stabilizer attempts to estimate unwanted motion and compensate it. Method and Smoothness control how aggressive that compensation is.

sections.title: Border strategy
sections.text: Stabilization often needs crop, scale or synthesized edge pixels; excessive smoothness can distort straight lines. Choose the least invasive method that solves the visible problem.

sections.title: Competing tasks
sections.text: A shot may first need a camera/point track before stabilization, or the shot may be stabilized only for a masking pass. Preserve an unchanged source for audit.

topics.experiment: Stabilize a ten-second handheld pan and check vertical edges for rubbery warping.
pitfalls: Do not assume every pan is unwanted motion.

topics.title: Tracked masks vs hand-roto
topics.summary: Automating vertices is useful only with deliberate quality review.

sections.title: Best candidates
sections.text: Fairly rigid textured shapes with predictable motion can be good mask-tracking targets. Large deforming hair edges generally need assisted or manual roto.

sections.title: Key cleanup
sections.text: Adjust path vertices only where visibly necessary, avoid unnecessary topology changes, and feather in a stable way over time.

sections.title: Fallback
sections.text: Point/planar trackers can drive a mask transform while a few manual keys adjust localized shape changes.

topics.experiment: Track a moving oval badge for three seconds and correct at least one deliberately induced drift.
pitfalls: Mask tracking does not infer hidden objects behind an occlusion perfectly.

topics.title: Brush and Clone Stamp in Layer panel
topics.summary: Painting has source-time and stroke-duration behavior.

sections.title: Context
sections.text: Select a suitable painting tool and work in Layer viewer. Source paint layers and Brush/Clone behavior depend on the Layer panel, Paint and Brushes controls.

sections.title: Temporal strokes
sections.text: Paint On Transparent and stroke Duration choices determine when and where marks appear. A fixed still frame repair may not remain aligned in later frames.

sections.title: Clone source
sections.text: Alt+click chooses a clone sampling source. Use small patches, animate/track where necessary and evaluate temporal texture consistency.

topics.experiment: Clone out a one-frame blemish, then expand the correction to ten frames with correct alignment.
pitfalls: Painting directly on a composited final view is not identical to editing a footage source.

topics.title: Content-Aware Fill video cleanup
topics.summary: Generate candidate replacement pixels after identifying the actual missing region.

sections.title: Define hole
sections.text: Use a tracked/animated mask to specify the region that needs replacement; ensure the correct alpha relationship before opening the Content-Aware Fill panel.

sections.title: Method and reference
sections.text: Choose the fill method suitable for the motion/texture. Reference Frames can give a clean example when automatic reconstruction struggles.

sections.title: Inspect variation
sections.text: Review every frame, watching warping, repetition and unwanted edge seams. A tracked clean plate or a more modest crop may be a better answer.

topics.experiment: Remove a small object and render a frame-by-frame contact sheet to catch flicker.
pitfalls: A good single still frame does not validate a fill over time.

topics.title: 2.5D layers and spatial depth
topics.summary: Position flat layers in 3D space to create depth cues.

sections.title: Z depth
sections.text: 2D layers occupy the comp plane; 3D layers add Z depth, orientation and material interactions. Move layers by different amounts in Z and view from a moving camera to create parallax.

sections.title: Separate planes
sections.text: A flattened photograph with all scene depth painted into one raster image cannot magically reveal hidden background behind foreground objects. Cut layers or create suitable gaps and patches.

sections.title: Lighting and renderers
sections.text: A 3D layer may accept lights/shadows depending on the renderer and its material settings. Use simple flat colors to diagnose shadows before importing textured assets.

topics.experiment: Build a three-plane parallax shot and check visibility of edges at both camera extremes.
pitfalls: 3D enabled layers are not automatically volumetric objects.

topics.title: Camera nodes, POI and projection
topics.summary: Move a camera with intention and inspect results in multiple views.

sections.title: One- and two-node cameras
sections.text: A one-node camera can be easier to orient directly. A two-node camera also has a Point of Interest; changing Position without considering POI can produce unexpected aiming changes.

sections.title: Zoom and depth
sections.text: Camera Zoom and focal length influence framing/perspective, while changing Z distances alters parallax. Do not confuse moving a flat layer closer with scaling it in 2D.

sections.title: Orbit rig
sections.text: Parent a camera to a Null positioned near the desired pivot for repeatable orbital movement. When editing camera POI, verify how parent transforms interact.

topics.experiment: Build one dolly and one orbit move and label which parameters changed.
pitfalls: Default Camera is a special view concept, distinct from an explicit camera layer.

topics.title: Classic 3D, Advanced 3D and Cinema 4D
topics.summary: Renderer choice defines the 3D features that actually calculate.

sections.title: Capabilities differ
sections.text: Advanced 3D supports imported models and advanced shading/material interactions, whereas Classic 3D and Cinema 4D renderer contexts serve different layer/geometry feature combinations.

sections.title: Performance modes
sections.text: Draft 3D and viewer preview modes trade interactivity for fidelity. Final frames need a deliberate check under the intended renderer and quality settings.

sections.title: Version gate
sections.text: After Effects 26.3 adds Advanced 3D in-engine depth of field, and 26.0 adds native parametric meshes; keep those out of a 25.6 test even if current Adobe Help screenshots display them.

topics.experiment: Put a native 3D layer in a simple comp and compare which renderer controls are enabled in each mode.
pitfalls: Render-time behavior can differ significantly from the viewport fast-preview display.

topics.title: GLTF/GLB/OBJ/FBX and environment lights
topics.summary: Use imported assets with predictable materials and scale.

sections.title: Model import
sections.text: 24.x introduced model import and Advanced 3D. 25.2 expanded FBX support and animated environment lights. Check exact supported features and texture naming on the files you actually import.

sections.title: Geometry vs layer
sections.text: A 3D model layer is a scene object; ordinary 2D effects are not equivalent to editing its mesh/material internals. Use 3D-specific controls and renderer options.

sections.title: Materials and lighting
sections.text: Use an HDR environment where appropriate, control exposure and orientation, and test shadow reception/casting. A model with missing UV textures may appear uniformly shaded or magenta/default.

topics.experiment: Import a simple neutral cube/GLB, light it, and record size, rotation and texture dependencies.
pitfalls: Substance SBSAR material workflows arrive with 26.x, not 25.6.

topics.title: 3D Camera Tracker and solved scenes
topics.summary: Recover a camera path only when footage contains enough useful 3D information.

sections.title: Analysis quality
sections.text: Good parallax and stable texture help the solve. Rotational-only motion, zoom, rolling shutter and motion blur may weaken results.

sections.title: Ground plane
sections.text: Choose tracked points that define a meaningful plane. Use a target region to create camera/solid/text and verify the object adheres across the whole shot.

sections.title: Failed solves
sections.text: Re-evaluate source quality, shot length and lens behavior. For one planar screen replacement, Mocha may be more direct than a full 3D camera solve.

topics.experiment: Track a short handheld room movement, create a ground-plane solid and watch it over 100 frames.
pitfalls: A solver can produce apparently plausible 3D points while failing the intended insert.

topics.title: Corner Pin and perspective insertion
topics.summary: A four-corner mapping targets planar surfaces.

sections.title: Planar geometry
sections.text: A surface defined by four tracked corners can accept an animated screen or sign; corner ordering and transform calibration are critical.

sections.title: Matching
sections.text: Add appropriate edge softness, brightness, surface tint, noise, source blur and movement to integrate replacement media.

sections.title: Diagnose drift
sections.text: Use a visible checkerboard or clear colored corners to spot track errors before replacing with a complex UI or text.

topics.experiment: Insert a 640×360 checkerboard onto a moving four-corner plane without visible slippage.
pitfalls: Perspective warp is not the same as a rigid layer transform with Position/Scale/Rotation.

topics.title: RGB, color profiles and grade order
topics.summary: Keep image corrections separate from color-science transforms.

sections.title: Correction then look
sections.text: Balance exposure, white point, contrast and saturation consistently before adding a style look. Shot matching becomes harder if each clip begins with arbitrary creative LUTs.

sections.title: Managed project
sections.text: ICC workflows convert source profiles into a designated working space; OCIO workflows use configured transforms. If working space is None, color management is not working as it would in a managed comp.

sections.title: Viewer vs file
sections.text: Display color management transforms a working image to the monitor; a rendered output transform targets delivery. These need not use the same profile/transform.

topics.experiment: Export a small test chart as unmanaged and Rec.709-managed files and inspect metadata and appearance.
pitfalls: Do not assume that turning monitor color management off edits the pixel values.

topics.title: 8/16/32 bpc and floating point
topics.summary: Project math precision differs from codec or source bit depth.

sections.title: Precision
sections.text: 8 bpc uses integer-like limited steps; 16 bpc provides finer channel precision; 32 bpc floating point supports values outside the display 0..1 range and is common for HDR/linear-light pipelines.

sections.title: No recovered highlights
sections.text: Changing a clipped 8-bit source to 32 bpc preserves further calculations but cannot restore highlights already clipped in the recording.

sections.title: Effect support
sections.text: Individual effects may have different 8/16/32 support. Verify through installed effect behavior and Adobe effect documentation before claiming that one effect is universal.

topics.experiment: Apply several Curves operations to a gradient in 8 bpc and 16 bpc and compare visible banding.
pitfalls: 32-bpc floating point project settings alone do not mean the H.264 output becomes 32-bit floating point.

topics.title: OCIO/ACES in a 25.6 project
topics.summary: Use the older available ACES configurations without importing 26.5-specific documentation.

sections.title: Color engine
sections.text: Project Settings → Color includes Adobe color managed and OpenColorIO-managed options in supported builds; choose the appropriate engine for the production pipeline.

sections.title: Config and transforms
sections.text: ACEScg is a working-space concept, not an output display transform. In OCIO choose configuration, source interpretation, working color space, viewing and output correctly.

sections.title: Version boundary
sections.text: 25.6 predates Adobe’s bundled ACES 2.0/OCIO 2.5.1 update in 26.5. A custom externally supplied config needs careful validation and does not justify claiming AE 25.6 has the newer built-in configs.

topics.experiment: Take one sRGB PNG, interpret it correctly in OCIO and export a Rec.709 display-targeted sample.
pitfalls: Do not accidentally apply a display transform twice, once in an effect and again at output.

topics.title: Expression evaluation and safe syntax
topics.summary: A property expression returns one calculated value at each time.

sections.title: Value vs action
sections.text: A property expression is computed as the composition renders. It changes a property value; it cannot arbitrarily add layers or save files.

sections.title: Functions
sections.text: Use time, value, wiggle(), ease(), linear(), clamp(), loopOut(), valueAtTime(), sourceRectAtTime(), toComp() and matching property types. On Position return a 2D/3D array as appropriate.

sections.title: Selection and errors
sections.text: Alt+click a stopwatch to create/remove an expression; the expression enable/disable switch is safer for temporary comparisons. Enable expression errors and resolve missing referenced effects or layers.

topics.experiment: Link one shape’s Rotation to another shape’s Position X coordinate via a scale mapping.
pitfalls: A pasted expression can silently refer to the wrong composition when copied across comps.

topics.title: JavaScript-like expressions, coordinates and values
topics.summary: Learn syntax, evaluation, and data dimensions rather than memorizing snippets.

sections.title: Types
sections.text: Numbers, arrays and strings differ. A 2D Scale returns `[x,y]`, Opacity returns one number, and Source Text can return a string or a compatible text style object.

sections.title: Property chain
sections.text: `thisComp.layer('NAME').transform.position` targets a concrete layer in current comp. `effect('Slider Control')('Slider')` reads a specific effect control; effect renaming changes the referenced path.

sections.title: Timing
sections.text: `time` is seconds, `framesToTime(n)` converts frames at context rate, and `posterizeTime()` alters expression sampling. `loopOut()` normally requires suitable keyed motion.

topics.experiment: Build a scale pulse driven by a Slider and toggle the slider from 0 to 100.
pitfalls: Variables declared inside an expression are not globally stored between frames.

topics.title: Sliders, points, angles, colors and dropdowns
topics.summary: Expose deliberate rig parameters on a named Null.

sections.title: Control interfaces
sections.text: Expression Controls include Slider, Angle, Point, Color and other types. A readable named Slider like Swing Degrees is much easier to tune than hardcoded numbers across 12 expressions.

sections.title: Reference correctly
sections.text: Use the pick whip to generate exact effect/property paths. If a control is deleted or renamed unexpectedly, expressions can error and freeze or use fallback behavior.

sections.title: Defaults and ranges
sections.text: Although a Slider can store a large range, clamp incoming values in expressions when out-of-range results would cause negative size or absurd motion.

topics.experiment: Make a master controller with Spin, Radius, Tint and Pause, then wire three layers.
pitfalls: A Slider is not automatically constrained to 0..100; clamp explicitly when required.

topics.title: CSV, JSON and AE data inputs
topics.summary: Make content replaceable while preserving animation structure.

sections.title: Formats
sections.text: CSV/TSV are suitable for flat tables and JSON for structured objects. A successful import does not guarantee the expression path to every nested field is what you assumed.

sections.title: Reference models
sections.text: `footage('file.json').sourceData` accesses JSON-like imported data; CSV/TSV may expose properties and dataValue access. Use the pick whip and inspect the actual imported shape.

sections.title: Failure modes
sections.text: Missing fields, wrong numeric types, commas in unquoted CSV fields and unexpected localized separators can break a template. Validate test rows including long names and zeros.

topics.experiment: Render three number cards from a short three-row data file.
pitfalls: Do not bake confidential contact information into broadly shared MOGRTs without permission.

topics.title: sourceRectAtTime and dynamic card padding
topics.summary: Text changes require layout that uses current bounds rather than fixed-width guessing.

sections.title: Bounds
sections.text: `sourceRectAtTime(time,false)` returns a text layer’s current layout bounds including left/top offsets. `width` and `height` are useful for a rectangular background size.

sections.title: Alignment
sections.text: The text bounding rectangle may be offset relative to anchor/Position. Align background and text in a shared coordinate context, or transform bounds with coordinate-conversion methods.

sections.title: Padding
sections.text: Add independent horizontal and vertical padding; test long, short and empty text. Set a reasonable maximum width or word wrapping to protect design.

topics.experiment: Build one name badge that gracefully handles a two-letter name and a 30-character name.
pitfalls: sourceRectAtTime does not automatically reposition a background around the text anchor.

topics.title: Essential Properties as instance controls
topics.summary: Different nested instances can expose and override selected controls.

sections.title: Master source
sections.text: Expose useful properties through Essential Graphics from an appropriate master comp; nested instances show the overrides as Essential Properties.

sections.title: Individual versions
sections.text: A reusable lower-third can use one source comp twice while individual instances have different title and color without altering shared internal animation.

sections.title: Maintainability
sections.text: Keep exposed properties few and well named. If required properties are missing or expressions refer elsewhere, the template can be difficult to customize.

topics.experiment: Make two instances of a one-source badge and change the name and color independently.
pitfalls: An override in one instance is not a permanent edit to the original source.

topics.title: Motion Graphics templates and protected timing
topics.summary: A .mogrt is a controlled reusable package, not merely an .aep saved under another extension.

sections.title: Interface design
sections.text: Expose controls editors actually need: text, colors, durations and a few positions. Test user error cases and descriptive names before publishing.

sections.title: Timing
sections.text: Protected Regions allow selected intro/outro sections to remain unchanged when a motion graphics template is retimed. Inspect transitions at minimum/maximum intended durations.

sections.title: Dependencies
sections.text: Font installations, licensed plugins and expressions can affect an exported template. Verify compatibility with the target editing application where possible.

topics.experiment: Create a 4-second MOGRT with intro, body and outro that maintains its intro/outro in an 8-second test.
pitfalls: A render or media proxy does not preserve MOGRT editability.

topics.title: Puppet deformation and mesh setup
topics.summary: Use pinned deformable geometry for flexible illustration and cutout work.

sections.title: Pins and triangles
sections.text: Pin positions deform an underlying mesh, which is generated according to source alpha and tool settings. Put stable pins at joints/support points, not one pin per pixel.

sections.title: Rig controls
sections.text: Overlap determines which portions move in front/behind in relevant puppet modes; Starch stiffens a region. Test with a flat fill and no extra glow/blur to see deformation clearly.

sections.title: Looping
sections.text: For a 2-second cycle, match first/last pin poses and smooth speed. Test outlines at each extreme for holes or crumpled triangles.

topics.experiment: Rig an arm with shoulder, elbow and wrist pins; make a clean wave.
pitfalls: A Puppet effect is not an automatic bone solver with awareness of anatomy.

topics.title: Particles, emitters and simulation
topics.summary: Keep rate, lifespan, force and size separate.

sections.title: Population
sections.text: Approximate live particle count at steady state = rate × lifetime, with caveats for frame sampling and survival settings. Changing Longevity and Birth Rate together can double-count a desired density.

sections.title: Movement
sections.text: Initial velocity, Gravity, Resistance and emitter position define trajectories. Explore physics controls one at a time, keeping all others constant.

sections.title: Integration
sections.text: A particle effect usually renders into the source layer’s context. For multiple depths, duplicate/precompose particle elements and use masks, mattes and lighting/glow appropriately.

topics.experiment: Build one spark emitter lasting 0.5 seconds with 2 seconds of fading particles.
pitfalls: Many native particle effects are 2.5D images, not real shaded 3D particles.

topics.title: Other simulation and stylize effects
topics.summary: Effects may generate pixels, distort existing pixels or simulate pseudo-physics.

sections.title: Families
sections.text: Shatter and CC Pixel Polly break pixels into chunks; CC Ball Action makes a point/ball grid; Foam/CC Bubbles generate liquid/bubble impressions; Turbulent Displace warps the existing source.

sections.title: Use by goal
sections.text: Choose a particle emitter for autonomous moving pieces, Displacement Map for controlled deformation, and a texture/pixelation effect for stylized source conversion.

sections.title: Parameter discovery
sections.text: Find each effect’s exact 25.6 parameter list in installed Effect Controls and Adobe effect-specific documentation. The guide cannot truthfully specify parameters for every bundled/third-party revision.

topics.experiment: Recreate the same stylized logo breakdown using Shatter and CC Pixel Polly; compare limitations.
pitfalls: Effects can be visually similar but have different layer size, sampling or cache behaviors.

topics.title: Render Queue decisions and preflight
topics.summary: Choose deliverable-first settings and verify the resulting asset.

sections.title: Choose output
sections.text: H.264 review media differs from editing mezzanine or RGBA master. Decide dimensions, frame rate, color space, audio, alpha and destination before opening Output Module.

sections.title: Render Settings
sections.text: Quality, resolution, frame blending, motion blur and time span are render decisions. Output Module chooses container, codec, channels, depth, audio, file path and color conversion.

sections.title: Verification
sections.text: Inspect the first, middle and last frames; play the complete audio; check output resolution, fps, file size and alpha in an external consumer. Record the settings with the deliverable.

topics.experiment: Deliver three variants of the same comp and document why each is appropriate.
pitfalls: Do not rely on an MP4 H.264 file for transparency.

topics.title: Containers, codecs, sequences and masters
topics.summary: Understand what the extension can and cannot promise.

sections.title: Container vs codec
sections.text: An .mp4 or .mov container can hold specific encoded video and metadata depending on the selected codec. ProRes/DNxHR/PNG/EXR differ in compression, color bit depth and alpha support.

sections.title: Image sequences
sections.text: A numbered PNG/EXR sequence preserves individual frames and may be resilient to interrupted renders, at the cost of many files and more management. Verify channel and color settings.

sections.title: Review vs mezzanine
sections.text: A small H.264 review is convenient; a high-quality intra-frame master or sequence is better for multiple rounds of effects/grading where supported by the pipeline.

topics.experiment: Render one 5-second RGBA element as a PNG sequence and confirm it recomposites cleanly in a fresh comp.
pitfalls: Setting alpha in an output module cannot add a channel that a format lacks.

topics.title: Collect Files and portability
topics.summary: An independently openable archive is the real deliverable test.

sections.title: Collection
sections.text: File → Dependencies → Collect Files copies referenced sources under chosen options and prepares a project. Confirm which proxies, unused items and plugin dependencies are included or omitted.

sections.title: Missing files
sections.text: Use Replace Footage and search folders to relink. Record stable relative subdirectories and verify no source still points to the old workstation.

sections.title: Team handoff
sections.text: Attach a README, screenshot/proof render and font/plugin list. Embed licensed third-party files only where your license permits.

topics.experiment: Reopen the collected copy with the original media drive disconnected.
pitfalls: A linked external Photoshop/Illustrator asset can be missing even when the project opens.

topics.title: RAM, disk cache and preview rate
topics.summary: Decide whether the bottleneck is decoding, rendering, memory or output.

sections.title: Cold vs warm preview
sections.text: The first pass calculates and caches frames. A replay may be far faster; changing a property can invalidate cached regions. Time only like-for-like comparisons.

sections.title: RAM and cache
sections.text: Memory preferences reserve RAM for other apps. Disk cache stores reusable intermediate frames on local storage; purging makes cached work disappear and may make the next playback slower.

sections.title: Multiframe
sections.text: When effects/plugins and resources permit, multi-frame rendering can render independent frames in parallel. Its gain depends on the shot, CPU, GPU, memory and media constraints.

topics.experiment: Time two previews before/after turning off an expensive effect; record whether the change helps cold and warm runs.
pitfalls: Do not blindly assign all RAM to AE at Windows’ expense.

topics.title: Cache levels, purging and invalidation
topics.summary: A cached preview is reused work, not a permanently rendered file.

sections.title: Viewer vs memory
sections.text: Green/blue cache indicators and preview panels tell you about cached ranges and conditions. Preview may re-render after color/render setting changes even when footage is unchanged.

sections.title: Disk vs RAM
sections.text: RAM cached frames are short-lived; persistent disk cache may survive a restart for eligible intermediates. The exact behavior depends on source/effect and cache settings.

sections.title: When to purge
sections.text: Purge only for a diagnostic reason, corruption or disk management; capture a baseline first. Running out of free disk space can produce errors unrelated to the actual comp design.

topics.experiment: Change only one Glow parameter and observe which frames need rerendering.
pitfalls: A preview cache does not substitute for a verified final exported master.

topics.title: Proxies, pre-renders and fast preview
topics.summary: Substitute cheaper pixels while retaining an exact source of truth.

sections.title: Footage proxies
sections.text: Assign a lower resolution/quality proxy to complicated sources and clearly indicate which file is active. Some export paths may use source or proxy depending on settings.

sections.title: Pre-render
sections.text: For a computationally expensive nested composition, generate a high-quality render, then substitute it for iteration. Keep original comps and a versioned render path.

sections.title: Final review
sections.text: Before delivery verify source/proxy switch and any downsampled raster effect resolutions. A Quarter view is a performance choice, not proof of final sharpness.

topics.experiment: Produce a small proxy of a 4K clip, edit a 1080 comp, and verify which frames use proxy vs original.
pitfalls: A proxy can hide scaling or codec artifacts that appear in the full-quality source.

topics.title: A structured debug decision tree
topics.summary: Reduce a failure to one reproducible cause.

sections.title: Picture missing
sections.text: Check active viewer, comp time, video switch, In/Out span, alpha, mask, matte, opacity, solo/shy, 3D camera, effect stack and codec decoding.

sections.title: Picture incorrect
sections.text: Compare ungraded sources, then source interpretation, effect order, color working/display/output transforms, precomp switches and full-quality render.

sections.title: Performance failure
sections.text: Test a short work area, one expensive layer, one plugin at a time and a different source codec. Do not diagnose a whole project only from the CPU/GPU model name.

topics.experiment: Take a deliberately broken comp and identify the exact stage that makes it wrong.
pitfalls: Multiple small causes can compound; one switch may not solve everything.

topics.title: Missing plugins, effects and unsupported version
topics.summary: A project can load without having the effect that produced a previous render.

sections.title: Diagnose source
sections.text: Check built-in Effects & Presets, Effect Manager, installed add-on version, licensing, Windows-only plugin paths and whether the effect debuted in 26.x.

sections.title: Avoid false fixes
sections.text: A missing plugin is not repaired by renaming an arbitrary different effect. Preserve the original project, replace intentionally, and compare the new render against a reference.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.text: 32-bpc, GPU acceleration, renderers and external plugin versions vary. Some old effects are marked Obsolete but may load older compositions for compatibility.

topics.experiment: Simulate missing effect by disabling one installed effect instance, save a test and document the visual fallback.
pitfalls: Do not attempt to run a 26.x-native project element inside 25.6 and assume it will downgrade.

topics.title: ExtendScript and project automation
topics.summary: Build deterministic and reversible changes from scripts.

sections.title: Object hierarchy
sections.text: JSX/ExtendScript scripts use the AE scripting API: application, project, items, compositions, layers, properties and render queue. This differs from time-evaluated expressions.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Use try/finally/undo groups, validate active project/item types and test on a versioned copy. Avoid unreviewed scripts from unknown sources.

sections.title: Repeatability
sections.text: Use explicit comp names, prefixes and logs. Keep external input CSV/JSON stable and back up files before automatic relinking, renaming or rendering.

topics.experiment: Write a no-op JSX report listing current comp names and save its result outside the source .aep.
pitfalls: JSX scripting is distinct from modern browser JavaScript modules or Node package installs.

topics.title: Missing media, absolute paths and Windows storage
topics.summary: Drive letters and renamed folders can silently disrupt a project.

sections.title: Paths
sections.text: If imported files move on disk, AE’s Project items can become missing. Relink footage from Project with Replace Footage, and inspect affected duplicates/sequences.

sections.title: Cache vs original
sections.text: Disk cache is disposable processed data; imported source assets are not. Do not delete Assets because AE cached a preview.

sections.title: Pack and transfer
sections.text: Collect Files with source folders, then test the collected copy by opening it from a different folder. Include any external audio, fonts, 3D textures and LUT references.

topics.experiment: Rename an asset folder in Windows Explorer, observe the missing footage, and relink correctly.
pitfalls: A project opened successfully can still have one or more missing media items.

topics.title: Repeatable production and QC workflow
topics.summary: Tie the individual skills into a dependable result.

sections.title: Define output first
sections.text: Agree on resolution, FPS, duration, codec, color, audio, alpha and revision rules before building layered animation. This determines composition settings and source requirements.

sections.title: Build in passes
sections.text: Block the story and timing, then implement graphics and track/roto, then add color, simulation and audio, finally handle render settings and QC.

sections.title: Review every layer of delivery
sections.text: A clean .aep, collected assets, fonts/plugins manifest, proof render and verified master are separate deliverables. Keep revision notes and a known-good prior version.

topics.experiment: Create a one-page checklist you can apply to any new client motion graphics job.
pitfalls: A single green check mark in Render Queue is not complete quality assurance.

topics.title: Final self-assessment and future practice
topics.summary: Demonstrate independent ability rather than recall of one memorized recipe.

sections.title: Foundations
sections.text: Build and animate a three-layer shape composition without referring to menus. If you need the guide, identify the exact missing concept rather than rewatching unrelated tutorials.

sections.title: Compositing and effects
sections.text: Make one alpha matte, one chroma key/rotoscope, one procedural transition, a controller-based rig and a correctly managed render.

sections.title: Maintenance
sections.text: Reopen a collected project on a different path, diagnose one deliberately missing source, and explain why later-version shortcuts do not apply in your installed build.

topics.experiment: Complete the 35th lesson, then modify three visual decisions without following the original exact steps.
pitfalls: A certificate is not meaningful without repeatable hands-on work.

topics.title: Footage source time vs comp time
topics.summary: Which source frame appears depends on interpretation, layer start, time stretch and remapping.

sections.title: Comp clock
sections.text: The timeline CTI measures time in the active composition. A source clip's first visible frame may be offset if the layer has an adjusted start time, In/Out or stretch.

sections.title: Remapped clock
sections.text: Time Remap keys specify the source timestamp to sample at a comp time. A reverse or freeze segment changes footage source sampling without moving the layer bar.

sections.title: Nested clocks
sections.text: A precomp layer samples an inner composition time; frame rates may differ, and fractional times can be involved. Always compare displayed source and comp frame counts.

topics.experiment: Make a clip show its original second 3 at comp second 1 without modifying the original media.
pitfalls: Source time must not be confused with keyframe timing.

topics.title: Frame-rate conversion and temporal sampling
topics.summary: Source FPS, composition FPS and output FPS are separate choices.

sections.title: Source interpretation
sections.text: Interpret Footage defines assumed source rate for certain media. Changing this is not the same as placing a 30-fps clip in a 24-fps comp.

sections.title: Sampling
sections.text: Compositions evaluate frames at their own FPS and may repeat/drop/blend sources if frame rates differ. Frame blending and pixel motion can interpolate but may create artifacts.

sections.title: Delivery
sections.text: Choose an output frame rate intentionally and verify final frame count, audio sync and timecode before handoff.

topics.experiment: Put a 30-fps clip into a 24-fps comp and compare frame blending off vs on during a fast pan.
pitfalls: Frame rate changes can make keyframe rhythms appear different at playback.

topics.title: Layer-based compositing and image order
topics.summary: Layers, alpha, mattes, blending and effects work together to produce pixels.

sections.title: Stack model
sections.text: In ordinary 2D, higher layers cover lower layers depending on their opacity, alpha and blending mode. An adjustment layer uses composited lower pixels as its image input.

sections.title: Opacity pipeline
sections.text: Source alpha, masks, effects and track matte controls can combine to set final coverage. Inspect RGB and alpha separately to find errors.

sections.title: Organizing passes
sections.text: For demanding shots, work on source cleanup, segmentation/keying, track integration, grade, then finishing grain/sharpness. Nest only when it clarifies render order.

topics.experiment: Build three overlapping colored shapes and explain precisely which pixels contribute at the center.
pitfalls: Blending two layers visually is not necessarily equivalent to creating alpha for downstream use.

recipes.title: 01 · Animated loading ring with Trim Paths
recipes.goal: Make a ring that draws itself without raster effects.
steps: Draw a shape ellipse with Fill set to None and Stroke to a visible color/width.
Inside Contents add Trim Paths and animate End from 0 to 100 over 16 frames.
For a spinning partial ring, set Start/End to reveal one arc, then animate Offset.
Add a Repeater or a second ring for additional visual structure, without unnecessary plugins.
Preview at target size to check line cap and antialiasing.
recipes.verify: Ring draws cleanly and is readable at one quarter of comp size.
recipes.fail: A fill may hide the open stroke if left enabled.

recipes.title: 02 · Handwriting from a traced mask
recipes.goal: Use the Stroke effect to reveal a line.
steps: Place scanned writing on a comp-sized solid or duplicated image as an image guide.
Draw one or several mask paths along the visible pen stroke in the correct order.
Apply Generate → Stroke, choose the mask(s) and Paint Style appropriate to the reveal.
Animate End from 0 to 100 over the intended write-on duration.
Use a white reveal matte or controlled Alpha Matte to reveal a separate textured ink layer when needed.
recipes.verify: Strokes appear in a plausible writing order and do not reveal undesired connecting lines.
recipes.fail: Stroke operates along masks, while Trim Paths operates on shape contents.

recipes.title: 03 · Logo reveal using a matte
recipes.goal: Animated shape reveals a graphic without destroying its pixels.
steps: Create a 1920×1080 24-fps composition and center a logo PNG with transparency.
Create a white rounded rectangle above it, longer than the logo and initially positioned left of the logo.
On the logo layer select the rectangle as an Alpha Matte source; use F4 if the TrkMat column is hidden.
Animate the rectangle from left of the logo to beyond its right edge in 20 frames. Add Ease Out and inspect alpha.
Place a second copy of the logo at low opacity underneath for a tasteful ghost trail, only if readability improves.
recipes.verify: The logo is never visibly stretched and is fully revealed by frame 20.
recipes.fail: If the entire rectangle renders, verify it is functioning as a matte source and that matte settings reference the intended layer.

recipes.title: 04 · Footage visible through moving text
recipes.goal: Use letters as an alpha matte.
steps: Create a new composition containing video and a large text heading on separate layers.
Place the text as the source of the footage layer track matte (Alpha Matte).
Animate the text’s Position or scale so the visible video window moves across the frame.
Add a background solid below the video. Fade the matte text after a hold while keeping the background visible.
Test Alpha Inverted Matte and compare which parts of the footage show.
recipes.verify: Footage is visible inside the glyphs only, without black squares.
recipes.fail: Do not mistake Screen blending for a matte.

recipes.title: 05 · Procedural cloud transition
recipes.goal: Combine noise, Levels and a matte reveal.
steps: Create a solid with Fractal Noise and animate its Evolution/Offset Turbulence.
Use Levels to increase contrast so it evolves into a thresholded black/white matte.
Apply the resulting precomp as a Luma Matte to reveal the new scene over the old.
Animate Levels Input Black/White to turn a partial cloudy mask into full coverage.
Test consistency at full frame dimensions and inspect whether the mask reverses unintentionally.
recipes.verify: Transition ends with completely visible second shot and no remaining first-shot pixels.
recipes.fail: If both pictures vanish, the luma matte direction may be inverted.

recipes.title: 06 · Depth-map-driven selective focus
recipes.goal: Blur one region more than another.
steps: Make a grayscale gradient with bright values in intended blurred regions.
Apply Camera Lens Blur to a duplicate of the footage and select the depth/blur map.
Tune Radius and map interpretation until background blur is stronger than the subject.
Feather the map and inspect the transition around the subject silhouette.
Compare to a global Gaussian Blur and evaluate render cost.
recipes.verify: Subject retains detail while distant region falls out of focus gradually.
recipes.fail: This is a 2D Camera Lens Blur workflow, not 26.3 in-engine Advanced 3D DOF.

recipes.title: 07 · Heat haze with Displacement Map
recipes.goal: Distort pixels using animated grayscale noise.
steps: Make a comp-sized solid, apply Fractal Noise, choose a broad smooth scale and reduce contrast.
Animate Offset Turbulence slowly to make the map drift; precompose it as MAP_HEAT.
Apply Displacement Map to the target footage, point it to MAP_HEAT and adjust displacement strengths modestly.
Mask the effect region or use a matte so heat haze appears near a specific source.
Add small blur/color variation only where necessary; compare map on/off over time.
recipes.verify: The background bends believably without an obvious repeating noise tile.
recipes.fail: A color noise map may need channel selection to avoid chaotic displacement.

recipes.title: 08 · Make a seamless time-remapped loop
recipes.goal: Avoid a one-frame black or phantom-frame flash.
steps: Import a visibly seamless 2-second clip into a 6-second comp.
Enable Time Remapping and inspect initial keyframes, especially end-duration key.
Set a key on the last valid frame and remove or correct the phantom duration-end key.
Add `loopOut('cycle')` expression to Time Remap and compare the repeated cycles frame by frame.
Check final frame and audio timing; Time Remap does not guarantee an inherently nonseamless source becomes seamless.
recipes.verify: No unexpected blank, duplicate or jump frame at loop boundaries.
recipes.fail: A mathematical loop cannot conceal mismatched first/last source artwork.

recipes.title: 09 · Staggered cards using Quick Offset
recipes.goal: A 25.4+ timeline technique to spread entrances in time.
steps: Create five shape cards stacked at the same center, each with a 10-frame Position entrance.
Select the intended layers in sequence, making sure selection order matches desired timing.
Hold Ctrl+Alt and drag the selected layer bars (Quick Offset) to distribute the group over time.
Inspect the earliest and latest start times; trim unwanted overlaps if necessary.
Preview and compare with manually offsetting keyframes only.
recipes.verify: Entrances are staggered without changing each layer’s internal animation.
recipes.fail: Quick Offset is a 25.4 feature; 26.0 Shift+bracket group-boundary shortcuts do not apply.

recipes.title: 10 · Animate to beats with markers
recipes.goal: Create rhythmic transitions without automatic beat-detection claims.
steps: Import and listen to a clean WAV on Timeline; show waveform with LL.
Add comp markers manually at the actual beat transients.
Align keyframe entrances 2 frames before a beat or exactly on beat depending on intended impact.
Use F9 and Graph Editor to make 6-frame ease-out impacts and longer holds.
Export and listen to rendered sound, checking whether markers match perceptual onsets.
recipes.verify: Every impact is perceptually synchronized in the exported movie.
recipes.fail: Waveform peak amplitude is not always the perceived musical beat.

recipes.title: 11 · Beat-reactive pulse
recipes.goal: Drive scale from audio-derived keyframes.
steps: Import an audio file and use Convert Audio to Keyframes.
Select a logo and add a 2D Scale expression referencing Audio Amplitude → Both Channels Slider.
Use a modest remap, e.g. `a=...; s=100+Math.min(20,a*1.5); [s,s];` with a valid pick-whip reference.
Preview with sound and observe peak reactions; smooth or cap peaks where needed.
Add a 10-frame opacity fade and export an audio-enabled review file.
recipes.verify: Logo scales gently with the sound and never collapses during quiet segments.
recipes.fail: Array dimensionality errors cause red expression warnings.

recipes.title: 12 · Keylight clean screen composite
recipes.goal: Isolate a foreground subject cleanly.
steps: Place evenly lit green-screen footage above a neutral background.
Apply Keylight (1.2); pick a green patch as Screen Colour.
Select Screen Matte view, tune Clip Black and Clip White gently, then return to Final Result.
Add garbage mask, Key Cleaner and Advanced Spill Suppressor where useful.
Check edges over black, white and saturated backgrounds, and verify 10 consecutive frames.
recipes.verify: Subject retains hair details without a green line or black halo.
recipes.fail: A crushed Screen Matte can erase semitransparent hair.

recipes.title: 13 · Tracked glowing outline
recipes.goal: Build glow from a clean traced contour.
steps: Create or track a mask path following the subject with as few stable vertices as possible.
Apply Generate → Stroke to a comp-sized solid and configure the path and width.
Precompose the stroke layer, duplicate it, blur one copy and add Glow to a duplicate.
Use a clean sharp core stroke above the soft bloom; tune opacities and blend modes.
Check motion frame by frame for outline detachment and edge aliasing.
recipes.verify: One sharp line remains visible inside the blur, and outline follows subject motion.
recipes.fail: A high blur on the only stroke layer produces a mushy and poorly defined outline.

recipes.title: 14 · Track a title onto moving footage
recipes.goal: Convert tracked pixels into a Null animation.
steps: Import a short shot with a stable high-contrast mark and create a comp from it.
In Tracker choose Track Motion and place Feature and Search Regions around the mark.
Track forward, correcting any drift frames. Create a Null and apply the tracking data to it.
Parent a title layer to the Null; position the text relative to the intended feature.
Add an outline/background to keep the title legible and preview each frame.
recipes.verify: The text follows the mark accurately for the full intended shot.
recipes.fail: A drifting null needs tracker correction; smoothing the title keys alone is not an accurate fix.

recipes.title: 15 · Roto Brush character cut-out
recipes.goal: Extract a moving person without a green screen.
steps: Open the subject video in Layer panel and activate Roto Brush.
Mark foreground and remove unwanted selected regions, starting at a good base frame.
Propagate through a 2-second segment, fixing errors around hands and head.
Use Refine Edge for hair and tune matte edge controls modestly; Freeze the result.
Place a background layer behind the cutout and render-check the complete segment.
recipes.verify: The subject is clean on at least two contrasting backgrounds.
recipes.fail: 25.6 does not include the 26.2 Object Matte tool; use available Roto Brush/Refine Edge.

recipes.title: 16 · Remove an object using Content-Aware Fill
recipes.goal: Generate a repair while retaining original footage.
steps: Duplicate the clip and draw a mask around the unwanted object.
Animate/track mask and set its mode to create the intended transparent hole.
Open Window → Content-Aware Fill and choose suitable range and Fill Method.
Generate Fill Layer; inspect every frame and try a reference frame if textures are inconsistent.
Render and compare to source, particularly near moving occlusions and boundaries.
recipes.verify: Object disappears without visible temporal pattern or seams.
recipes.fail: Content-Aware Fill may give temporally unstable texture; a clean plate may work better.

recipes.title: 17 · Simple camera orbit rig
recipes.goal: Use a Null as a stable camera pivot.
steps: Create a comp with three 3D solids at different depths.
Create a 2-node camera and an appropriately positioned 3D Null.
Parent the camera to the Null and animate the Null’s Y rotation 0→30 degrees.
Adjust camera local Position so subject stays framed; verify target/Point of Interest behavior.
Render in the intended 3D renderer and compare to a Position-only camera move.
recipes.verify: Subject remains readable while background layers show depth shift.
recipes.fail: Incorrect pivot placement can make a camera orbit resemble uncontrolled zoom.

recipes.title: 18 · Parallax from a still photograph
recipes.goal: Cut source artwork into near/mid/far planes.
steps: Prepare a background image and two transparent foreground cutouts from the same photo.
Import each as a layer, enable 3D and spread them apart on the Z axis while preserving intended screen placement.
Create a camera and make a short lateral dolly/arc that reveals a depth difference.
Extend hidden background under the foreground silhouette to prevent holes.
Add subtle light/blur in the appropriate renderer and preview both camera extremes.
recipes.verify: The foreground moves more than background without revealing empty cutout edges.
recipes.fail: Scaling a single flat photograph is not real parallax.

recipes.title: 19 · Replace a moving sign/screen
recipes.goal: Map a replacement layer into four moving corners.
steps: Choose a shot of an almost planar screen or poster with visible texture.
Open bundled Mocha AE from the effect integration, draw a planar region and track the shot.
Set/verify a planar surface with the correct corner order; transfer corner pin data using the integration available in 25.6.
Place a bold checkerboard into the replacement comp and inspect alignment at each frame.
Replace the checkerboard with the desired screen contents; match blur, exposure and noise.
recipes.verify: Checkerboard corners remain anchored and final insert has no glaring seams.
recipes.fail: Perspective slippage usually indicates an unstable plane or the wrong corner calibration.

recipes.title: 20 · Controlled RGB channel split
recipes.goal: Make an aberration effect using channel routing.
steps: Precompose a source with correct alpha, then duplicate it into three layers.
Apply Shift Channels so each copy isolates red, green or blue, and combine with Add where appropriate.
Offset red slightly left and blue slightly right, leaving green centered.
Use a mask/adjustment where the effect should occur, rather than displacing the whole frame continuously.
Check seams, alpha and color clipping at Full resolution.
recipes.verify: Aberration appears near high-contrast edges without introducing a giant invisible background.
recipes.fail: With alpha artwork, additive recomposition can unintentionally alter transparency.

recipes.title: 21 · JSON-driven statistics title
recipes.goal: Load external numbers into Source Text.
steps: Create a UTF-8 JSON file with a simple `{"team":"North","score":42}` object.
Import it into the project and create a Source Text expression using `footage('stats.json').sourceData.score` with a valid data path.
Convert the numerical result to a string, label it with a title and position it inside a shape card.
Use `sourceRectAtTime` to auto-size card background with 20 pixels of padding.
Change JSON to a longer team label and verify the design remains readable.
recipes.verify: Values update after reloading external data and remain properly aligned.
recipes.fail: Always check JSON syntax and exact field names.

recipes.title: 22 · Reusable lower third with Essential Properties
recipes.goal: Separate animation from editable name/role content.
steps: Build a 1920×1080 child comp with two text layers and a shape-rectangle background.
Place all layers under a controller Null, then animate entrance over 10 frames and exit over 10 frames.
Open Essential Graphics, expose name text, role text and primary fill color with descriptive labels.
Nest the comp twice in a master; override the name/role independently using Essential Properties.
Export a MOGRT after checking typography bounds and protected regions when appropriate.
recipes.verify: Two independent instances show different content with the same timing and art direction.
recipes.fail: If one instance unexpectedly changes both names, you edited the shared source rather than an override.

recipes.title: 23 · Puppet waving flag
recipes.goal: A flexible loop from a static transparent flag.
steps: Import a transparent flag shape and inspect its alpha edges.
Add Puppet pins at fixed pole edge and on two flowing sections of fabric.
Animate mid and tip pins across three poses over two seconds.
Use stiffness controls when necessary to avoid folding the pole itself.
Copy the first pose to the loop end and smooth all movements.
recipes.verify: Flag waves smoothly and the pole edge stays visually stable.
recipes.fail: Too many pins fight each other and create crumpling.

recipes.title: 24 · Native particle burst
recipes.goal: A measured CC Particle World experiment.
steps: Apply CC Particle World to a suitable comp-sized solid.
Set Birth Rate to a low visible rate and key it to 0 after the first 12 frames.
Set Longevity to about 2 seconds; choose a particle style and initial velocity and gravity.
Adjust emitter position so particles emerge from the logo center.
Add gentle Glow after the particle effect and preview at actual playback speed.
recipes.verify: No particles are born after the burst ends, but earlier particles die naturally.
recipes.fail: Birth Rate 0 stops new particles; it does not kill those already alive.

recipes.title: 25 · Transparent master and color check
recipes.goal: Deliver usable compositing assets.
steps: Make a 48-frame comp with a moving semi-transparent circle over an empty comp background.
Choose Render Queue Output Module format/codec supporting alpha; set RGB+Alpha and appropriate alpha interpretation.
Render a lossless/near-lossless master or numbered PNG sequence with intentional color settings.
Import the result into a fresh comp over dark blue and hot pink backgrounds; inspect edge transparency.
Render a separate H.264 review file with a solid background; label it as a non-alpha review.
recipes.verify: The alpha master has transparent edges, and the MP4 review is correctly labeled.
recipes.fail: An .mp4 file may look like an alpha preview in AE but will not preserve ordinary transparency.

recipes.title: 26 · Collect Files handoff test
recipes.goal: Prove that your project is portable.
steps: Save the final project with descriptive version and output names.
Choose File → Dependencies → Collect Files and create a fresh folder that contains the project and required footage.
Add a README of fonts, third-party effects, scripts, LUTs and manual configuration notes.
Move the collected folder to a different Windows directory and reopen its project file.
Render a tiny proof frame; confirm it matches the pre-collection output and uses the new source paths.
recipes.verify: Project reopens from collected directory and produces identical proof frames.
recipes.fail: Collect Files does not install fonts or purchase plugin licenses.

recipes.title: 27 · Final 10-second integrated sequence
recipes.goal: Practice the entire production pipeline with one coherent composition.
steps: Create a 24-fps 10-second comp and organized project folders; establish color and output format.
Make a two-second alpha-matte animated title with a readable hold.
Add a three-card stagger using controlled easing and a Null; build one reusable editable title element.
Place either a tracked element or roto/keyed person over a short plate; inspect edges in motion.
Add a procedural 2-second transition and final text, synchronize audio, then render MP4 and an appropriate master.
Collect Files, reopen the collected project and write a self-critique of three improvements.
recipes.verify: Both render and portable project exist, with no one-frame flashes or missing media.
recipes.fail: A capstone is not complete until the collected source can be reopened.

effects.name: Camera Lens Blur
